## A Violence
******Paula Bohince**
Princeton University Press ($17.95)
_by Erick Verran_
The patchwork story of _A Violence_, Paula Bohince’s fourth collection of poetry, is one of being “no longer anonymous.” Out of “a bosom / of incense and secrecy,” we’re thrown into a world of disordered nerves and trauma, where a therapist drives “to Jawbone in her Honda” at the beck of voices and insurance agents with cameras hide in the grass. (In winking acknowledgement, Bohince throws in _The Conversation_, Francis Ford Coppola’s psychological thriller about a paranoid surveillance expert.) Seeking calm in a wifi-connected society, Bohince nods off under a canopy of digital rain. Through the wreckage of her brain, images dart to and fro like damselfish:
> An ultraviolet urchin _(plantary,  
>   
> local)_ was lulling unaware  
>   
> in waves eternal  
>   
>   
> when Mari’s email turned to  
>   
> stardust, touching a satellite’s face  
>   
> for a nano, then  
>   
>   
> crystallizing on Earth  
>   
> in the absolute blackness  
>   
> of a laptop’s clamshell,  
>   
>   
> in zone difference. The Pacific  
>   
> tugged its trash as I   
>   
> dreamt, as the crab  
>   
>   
> awoke shameless, shrugging  
>   
> off its burial, beginning again.
Bohince’s sympathy has a wide cast, with a soft spot for down-and-outers and the heartbreak of those who perform thankless labor, such as barmaids mothering drunks (“our charges, sealed in / submarine darkness”) or the aunt “who kept house / for a family and got to visit the cape once / a year to mind the children.” Her use of enjambment is quietly devastating, as are her still lifes, evocative arrangements composed of animal and mineral: rain-soaked donkeys waiting amid the shriveled blooms of “druidic elderflowers” in a darkened barn, an octopus at the bottom of the Atlantic that “cradles / itself to sleep in all of its arms.” In a disgusting bucket, bony xylophones dangle from fish heads, their eyes—like ours, seeing too much too soon—permanently shocked open.
texts.8:
## A Violence
Bohince also has an ear for sayings (“sobs of snow,” “ignorant as sunshine”) that feel age-old, handed down, as durable as the peals of a sixteenth-century bell:
> Motes  
>   
> now, my people, but a melody guided us   
>   
> as it once brightened the edge of a Slovenian lake  
>   
>   
> where a girl held her hem  
>   
> and waded in, our lives  
>   
> inside of her and inside of him, the one  
>   
> who held out his hand, the husband.
That vanished colony of adults, wiped out like Roanoke by the usual diseases, haunts its lone survivor. “Sure, I was eternal,” Bohince admits, floating through “tipsy polka,” rhubarb, wild carrot. There’s humor, too, and the promise of new beginnings: when a friend breastfeeds a newborn, the speaker coos at it in Gaelic.But the poet is at her recollective best when she allows herself a certain breadth to say things at length instead of condensing. A lot in _A Violence_ is as thick as Campbell’s soup:
> Was a swell commandant: drink up, sleep. She’d   
>   
> relinquished the vampy black and absconded to her toddler  
>   
> color _(muddy sunset)_ as we, one from each grief stage,   
>   
> commissioned to flock her, petal’d her pale strapless,  
>   
> pressed the appliqué along her spine with dancer’s glue,   
>   
> all funds sunk into that silk, hence the wan hors d’oeuvres,  
>   
> sheepish flasks, _White Album_ on a loop.
While the weeping in _A Violence_ may be copious (“then the world ordered _Weep_, and I wept”), one discovers there is no end to experience, scavenged from the macabre and quotidian in equal measure. Even simulacra can instruct, like a gold-plated earring tarnished “from its season in Hell” or when flakes land unfeelingly on the iris of a taxidermied deer. Bohince’s tender, Lowellian blend of family lore and remembrance comes together in “The Skunk,” a poem about her late mother, with stunning pathos:
texts.9:
## A Violence
> I went wild,  
>   
> memorizing her the way others did _Ozymandias_.  
>   
>   
> One Christmas, when I was grown, I wanted to cook for her  
>   
> the meal of a lifetime. To say, _Mom, This is living. This is love._ _Feel it._ Flakes of salt on closed lips of asparagus,  
>   
> duck limp-necked on a secondhand platter.  
>   
>   
> She kept her head down and ate fast, with shame, and gave me  
>   
> before leaving melted together wedding rings,  
>   
> hers and my dad’s. Amulet for I don’t know what.  
>   
> Pain-medallion. Coin for the underworld.  
>   
>   
> In the New Year, I flattened beneath  
>   
> the dentist’s lead apron and thought of her (I’m always  
>   
> thinking of her), her red pilled sweater, how she looked around  
>   
> at the candles, her face scorched from crying.
Like Proteus “in a high-up cave,” Bohince seems to carry within her a range of avatars, from “shirtless carpenters . . . on their summer jobs, / oiled as horses,” to Diego Velázquez and named lambs. Except, despite an homaging parenthetical to Elizabeth Bishop, Bohince more often resembles a less ornate version of Gjertrud Schnackenberg, whose gilded touch occasionally treats a beloved memory as grandparents used to a pair of baby’s shoes. Still, it’s undeniable that Bohince has a knack for writing disaster. Trying to mollify “the past, whatever that is,” she has been grieving in reverse, sketching whatever’s left of yesteryear in a manner that, however nostalgia-tinged, is mostly stoical—meaning “lighter, rinsed of those associations” which mattered profoundly once upon a time.

He takes tropes and uses them to rope-a-dope the reader; he springs the traps laid by convention and the strictures of form in order to dictate his own course, to establish new norms. In particular, Whitehead repurposes ready-made narratives to explore underrepresented areas of Black experience; he consistently commits to the bit and then twists it, finding emotional resonances where you’d least expect them.

Along the way, Whitehead celebrates, in deliberately unsentimental fashion, the variety of Black ingenuity and splendor on offer in marginalized circles.

“In place of standardized hardboiled crime fiction, with its emphasis on formula and procedure,_Cool Machine_ is a sophisticated meditation on Black masculinity, aging, and unsanctioned political resistance (Du Bois defines crime as ‘the open rebellion of an individual against his social environment,’ which could apply to revolutionaries or gangsters). Rather than standard thievery, this novel considers another kind of seizure—what it means to lose time, and thus the potential to change, even as everything around you is being constantly reframed. Witnessing their development is the gift of getting to know characters on layaway over nine easy installments. But the insurance afforded by a series can also expose its inherent flaws. As in the first two novels, Carney and Pepper are put through the wringer, but I never felt like they were truly in trouble. The tropes of the crime novel wear thin, with its grim foreshadowing and prodigious exposition. The three-novella structure is sometimes predictable, with its movie-of-the-week rhythm, which requires resolution every hundred pages or so. But these are misdemeanors, easy to overlook.
…
“Although it’s a novel, I’m beginning to think of _Cool Machine_ as a counterhistory of Harlem’s underworld, one that surprises because it prioritizes human frailty and imagination. Regarding the fate of one mislaid item on the move in this final novel, we learn that there is a crucial two-week period that goes unaccounted for between what happens to the object and the revelation of its fate. The mystery of what exactly occurs in the interim belongs to one character alone—not even the reader knows what went down with real detail, though we can imagine. Here, Whitehead’s joking writing instruction comes in handy. Indeed, what isn’t said is important. In this case, some of the really good stuff happens off the page, in the minds of readers and in the hearts of rogue personalities we can’t quite pin down.”
–Niela Orr on Colson Whitehead’s**_Cool Machine_**(_Vulture_)

“But for those alarmed by the turbulence of midlife, the writer Valeria Luiselli’s novels offer a refreshingly different perspective. ‘I once read in a book by Saul Bellow that the difference between being alive and dead is just a matter of viewpoint,’ the narrator of Luiselli’s debut novel,_Faces in the Crowd_, recalls. She goes on to explain that the ‘living look from the center outward, the dead from the periphery to some kind of center.’ According to this worldview, the middle of life, far from a time to reset yourself, is the crux of human existence. And in Luiselli’s new novel,_Beginning Middle End_, it’s also where the messiest, most interesting, and most exciting parts of a story occur.
…
“Luiselli has long been intrigued by literary boredom._Beginning Middle End_, like all of her novels, goes without what its protagonist calls the ‘corset of plot.’ By no means does it lack drama—see: impending lover, maybe-sick mother; because this is Sicily, there’s also a looming volcano—but traditional story does not drive the novel forward. As it winds down, Luiselli does not resolve any of its questions (Is the mom all right? Will the narrator be able to write again?) but instead hands the narrative from the protagonist to her daughter. The novel’s final section takes on the daughter’s voice, and in its last lines, the daughter arbitrarily declares her mother’s book over: ‘This is the story,’ she says. ‘It has a beginning, a middle, and an end, and this is the end.’ By rejecting the myth of beginning again and the idea that endings are inherently meaningful, Luiselli highlights the fascination of the middle.
It’s a bold approach to life, more than literature. In the traditional arc of a book, of course, the ending can come only once. A beginning, meanwhile, sets a story’s tone and stakes. It tells the audience whom and what to care about, and creates, ideally, a sense of expectation and intrigue. Beginnings, in short, exist to make you want to read middles. In life, this can be tougher to accept; it’s hard to be in the middle, twisting between life and death.
texts.3:
Still, as my grandfather used to say, it beats the alternative. He was talking about dying, but also, I wouldn’t want to be (or have) a newborn forever, or ditch my husband after the honeymoon, or quit my job as soon as a challenge arises. Forging onward can sound duller and bleaker than launching a new life—hence, I think, the appeal of stories about multiverses—but in fact, it leads directly to the interesting stuff._Beginning Middle End_ knows that the first and last words in its title are just necessities. It’s the center, where life flails on, that counts.
–Lily Meyer on Valeria Luiselli’s_**Beginning Middle End**_(_The Atlantic_)

## The Dissidents: Autocrats! Vigilantes! Communists! ... and Cartoonists!
******Derf Backderf**
Abrams ($29.99)
_by Chris Barsanti_
“I’m not a Marxist, let’s get that out of the way,” Derf Backderf notes at the start of his latest graphic novel, _The Dissidents_. “I am, however, a cartoonist.” This may sound defensive, something an artist feels is required as a throat-clearer in reactionary times to ensure they are not dismissed as some radical or ideological simpleton. But though the book is about the U.S. government’s intimidation of a cadre of Red-aligned cartoonists in the early 20th century, Backderf’s interest is less in their political beliefs than in the frighteningly unconstitutional nature of the pressure campaign against them.
_The Dissidents_ is an illuminating slice of art history knitted into a knuckleduster of a story about the mostly immigrant agitators, organizers, and pamphleteers who thronged America’s industrial cities at the start of World War I. It’s a big shift from Backderf’s recent graphic novels such as _Kent State: Four Dead in Ohio_(Abrams, 2020), which even when political have been mostly autobiographical. Here, he takes a page from fellow Ohioan graphic novelist Harvey Pekar, whose _Students for a Democratic Society: A Graphic History_ (Hill and Wang, 2008) also illuminated the struggles of a faction of Americans who tried to hold back the tide of militarism.
Though his book is filled with a roster of historical figures, Backderf invents a fictional protagonist as the reader’s entry point to the story. Joe Hertle is an earnest German-American from Cleveland—one of the ethnic “hyphenates” whose loyalty and Americanness is always in question—who aspires to be a great cartoonist like those he sees in his favorite magazine, _The Masses_. In many ways, _The Dissidents_ is a love letter to this short-lived radical publication, whose gorgeous and striking artwork Backderf liberally reproduces throughout. While high-minded in its denouncements of capitalist excess and the pointless butchery of World War I, the magazine was not an intellectual exercise but instead aimed at the everyday readers whose lives and livelihoods were under threat.

## The Dissidents: Autocrats! Vigilantes! Communists! ... and Cartoonists!
Hertle is galvanized by his first direct encounter with dissident politics. Attending a Wobbly labor rally led by “Big Bill” Haywood that turns into a pitched battle when police and private goons try to bust it up, Hertle is grievously wounded. Looking to meet his heroes, Hertle leaves for New York; there he works his way into the cell of underground radicals and aesthetes publishing _The Masses_ while being tailed by government agents. It’s a heady flutter of parties and verbal jousting in cafes where the frenetically idealistic spirit is further intensified by the looming threat of President Wilson’s crackdown, like coal being crushed into a diamond. In case readers weren’t already reminded of Warren Beatty’s _Reds_, John Reed, Louise Byrant, and Emma Goldman make bold cameos before Hertle’s starstruck eyes.
Like nearly all stories of political movements, _The Dissidents_ ends in tragedy and disillusion. Wilson’s crackdowns on “sedition” used the excuse of World War I to imprison, deport, silence, and crush (spiritually, economically) his opponents like at _The Masses_. Backderf’s style becomes darker as the story trends downbeat. His crisply tactile figures and sharp shadows are used to illustrate the police brutally rounding up and bystanders jeering at all the “radical hyphenates” targeted by 1919’s ignominious swell of authoritarian xenophobia.
There’s beauty aplenty in _The Dissidents_, which stands as a visually eloquent testament to the power of creativity, alongside a realistic appraisal of the limitations of even the most finely-wrought agitprop. Backderf’s insight is not to separate art from action in this poignant, evocative portrait of hope in the face of oppression.

## Is Beauty Good
******Rosalind Belben**
New York Review of Books ($17.95)
_by Julia Laurel Mueller_
In the last three years, three novels by English writer Rosalind Belben originally published between 1974 and 1989 have been republished. Since it’s been nineteen years since her most recent book, _Our Horses in Egypt_(Chatto & Windus, 2007), won the James Tait Black Award, what accounts for this flurry of renewed interest? Perhaps it suggests a fresh appeal in how this resolutely eccentric writer—potentially for anyone, definitely not for everyone—makes readers feel at home in some of the least accommodating parts of language. In this age of algorithms and large language models, Belben’s voices are stubbornly small, lingering, and unassimilable.
The new edition of _Is Beauty Good_ offers an opportunity to encounter anew Belben’s 1989 novel composed of a chorus of unidentified voices. The title is a drifting incantation in the form of a question, the absence of punctuation holding it back from ever being answerable. Its three simple words, recurring at intervals throughout the novel, allow Belben to suspend the title’s meaning, and to keep it in play.
In her introduction to this edition, German writer and translator Esther Kinsky finds a quality “between the lines” in Belben’s book. With no exact verbal equivalence in English, _Fremde_ means “somewhere between strange and foreign and alien.” On that basis, you might think the novel is difficult, but it is not really a novel of ideas—it never asks for strenuous interpretation. Rather, it invites us to take it as it is, to enter into the sensuous private life of words. Never finished with its question, it is not a book to look to for answers.

## Is Beauty Good
Kinsky, who ventures that _Fremde_ is “a much underrated feature of human life,” is the perfect person to write this introduction: She expresses an instinctive sympathy for Belben’s sensibility, and notes that many of the novel’s voices speak from West Berlin, or from “Alpine regions where German is spoken.” German words sometimes “crop up, without comment or translation.” The “foreignness” which is part of _Fremde_ becomes a way of emphasizing not only these German interlopers among English words, but the foreignness of language itself, the bedrock at which all language is foreign. Even our own language is not always _ours_ when we are _its_, and vice-versa. Belben dignifies this contradiction by a method of perpetual shifting and displacement—as when one of the voices tells us of a “companion’s mother” with a “disorder, a facial cataclysm”: “it redefined her thoughts, her world, her circumstances . . . But one had to look away while it was happening.”
We are never formally introduced to any of the figures (I hesitate to say characters) in the novel, yet this lack enables a rare form of intimacy, inviting us into the open air of a collective mind sifting through language. Without enforcing identity, Belben’s voices become disarmingly (and sometimes alarmingly) open to us, and we become vulnerable to them. To be a reader in the company of this motley collection of souls is also to find oneself welcomed in without formality. Belben’s sentences, and the voices speaking them, are forthright and somehow familiar, yet always a little aslant too—enough to keep us from ever making that self-satisfied sound of comprehending profundity. One voice recalls a dog named Florus in the chapter named for him: “His face would change, as emotion transforms one, when a smoothing or a wrinkling occurred in his thoughts.” That slip from “his” to “one” and back to “his” conveys the characteristic mutability of Belben’s syntax.

## Is Beauty Good
Belben has been compared to Virginia Woolf, yet her prose also brings to mind that of Samuel Beckett—the words rattling around in the skull; the eruptive, uncouth tones; the profane sense of humor. Where Beckett’s style proceeds by economy and recombination, however, Belben cultivates a multiplicity of inner voices. The only boundaries between these voices are the chapters.
“Flowers have no sense of danger,” the voice of the final chapter announces, after wondering whether “only the plants and flowers can know what’s beautiful.” Flowers, those almost universal emblems of unobjectionable beauty, become the only ones who might actually know what the word means, though of course they themselves are wordless. The novel often seems to be working out ways to communicate what is, strictly speaking, non-communicable. The simple longings of the speaker of a chapter called “Exile” reverberate through the whole: “Let me have a garden, let me have a dog, let me have privacy.”
Fortunately, Belben’s is a confiding privacy. The chapters are grouped into three larger sections, the third bearing the subtitle “_from the deaf man’s conversation book_”—a phrase that suggests, in Belben’s inimitable idiom, a condition of language, that uncanny medium in which we move very slowly toward a fragile, provisional understanding of what we might mean. “It’s a toss-up, whether silence is better,” she writes. _Is Beauty Good_ is an unnerving testament to our deepest inarticulacies, yet somehow Belben holds it out to us with an endearing warmth. It’s by this grace that we can read without despair, and even with a peculiar joy.

## Without Terminus: untraining an archive
******chaun webster**
Graywolf Press ($18)
_by Walter Holland_
In his brilliant new nonfiction work _Without Terminus: Untraining an Archive,_ poet chaun webster tells us that “the black historical is already the hauntological.” Ostensibly a memoir about his maternal grandfather Reginald Jerry Clark, who worked as a porter for the Great Northern Railroad for twenty-five years, the book becomes a kind of ghost story, a history of an absence, by following this insight.
An inquisitive, empathetic thinker, webster explores the paradoxes of writing about his grandfather, who remains a mystery to him except for a few artifacts. Setting out on this archival trail, webster entangles us in a broader context of Black genealogy, history, and identity. A sleuth, historian, sociologist, semiotician, and intimate memoirist all at once, he asks at the start of the book:
> what does it mean to be gone? or to have so much difficulty in proving the here-ness of my kin? when history has arrived to me fractured already my instinct it to engage in a recovery mission. but I am unsure if this is one.
With continuous self-inquiry, webster employs digressions ranging from etymological inquiries to critical spatial discourse analysis to revisualize and restore his grandfather’s missing history. One such digression involves the word that underlies his grandfather’s work as a porter, an obliging role that demanded endlessly long hours without a break, thus tiring his body, ruining his health, and basically sacrificing his life to raise his family:
> to _com port_ as intransitive verb is to be fitting, often in terms of behavior: the porter _comports_ to the directive. its prefix com-_with,_ the Latin word _comportare_ meant _to bring together._ coincide, cohere, correspond, rhyme. and what is forcibly being brought together by language? what happens when the body is inconsistent with the container it is violently being required to correspond with? when it will not comport . . .

## Without Terminus: untraining an archive
webster, who has previously published two award-winning poetry collections, displays an especially imaginative virtuosity in _Without Terminus,_ showcasing his skill at word graphics and visual rhetoric. Perhaps the most visually arresting part of the book is a series of pages in which webster analyzes the only written account of his grandfather he can find. Clark’s obituary in the local newspaper is headlined “St. Paul Man Dies After / Illness of Short Duration.” He took ill on a streetcar on his way to work where he had been employed for some time as a red cap, and he was taken to Ancker Hospital where “he died an hour later. Mr. Clark was well-known throughout the Twin Cities and had many friends. The cause of his sudden death has not been determined.” webster responds with the following two-page spread:
webster’s process involves repetition and reexamination from myriad textual angles and typographical approaches, as if to create engrams of his conflicted memories and abiding yearning for familial closure and belonging. Toward the book’s end, he explains what compelled him to write this work: “the holes in your memory, your memory being against narrative composition, discontinuous threads you’ve attempted to braid and tear apart again. what do you remember? what don’t you remember?”
Form and content in _Without Terminus_ are so complexly aligned that patient rereadings will illuminate the cultural codes and social conventions that have historically created Black American identity. Meanwhile, chaun webster is to be commended for having broadened the conversation.

## A Violence
******Paula Bohince**
Princeton University Press ($17.95)
_by Erick Verran_
The patchwork story of _A Violence_, Paula Bohince’s fourth collection of poetry, is one of being “no longer anonymous.” Out of “a bosom / of incense and secrecy,” we’re thrown into a world of disordered nerves and trauma, where a therapist drives “to Jawbone in her Honda” at the beck of voices and insurance agents with cameras hide in the grass. (In winking acknowledgement, Bohince throws in _The Conversation_, Francis Ford Coppola’s psychological thriller about a paranoid surveillance expert.) Seeking calm in a wifi-connected society, Bohince nods off under a canopy of digital rain. Through the wreckage of her brain, images dart to and fro like damselfish:

>   
> local)_ was lulling unaware  
>   
> in waves eternal  
>   
>   
> when Mari’s email turned to  
>   
> stardust, touching a satellite’s face  
>   
> for a nano, then  
>   
>   
> crystallizing on Earth  
>   
> in the absolute blackness  
>   
> of a laptop’s clamshell,  
>   
>   
> in zone difference. The Pacific  
>   
> tugged its trash as I   
>   
> dreamt, as the crab  
>   
>   
> awoke shameless, shrugging  
>   
> off its burial, beginning again.
Bohince’s sympathy has a wide cast, with a soft spot for down-and-outers and the heartbreak of those who perform thankless labor, such as barmaids mothering drunks (“our charges, sealed in / submarine darkness”) or the aunt “who kept house / for a family and got to visit the cape once / a year to mind the children.” Her use of enjambment is quietly devastating, as are her still lifes, evocative arrangements composed of animal and mineral: rain-soaked donkeys waiting amid the shriveled blooms of “druidic elderflowers” in a darkened barn, an octopus at the bottom of the Atlantic that “cradles / itself to sleep in all of its arms.” In a disgusting bucket, bony xylophones dangle from fish heads, their eyes—like ours, seeing too much too soon—permanently shocked open.

## A Violence
Bohince also has an ear for sayings (“sobs of snow,” “ignorant as sunshine”) that feel age-old, handed down, as durable as the peals of a sixteenth-century bell:
> Motes  
>   
> now, my people, but a melody guided us   
>   
> as it once brightened the edge of a Slovenian lake  
>   
>   
> where a girl held her hem  
>   
> and waded in, our lives  
>   
> inside of her and inside of him, the one  
>   
> who held out his hand, the husband.
That vanished colony of adults, wiped out like Roanoke by the usual diseases, haunts its lone survivor. “Sure, I was eternal,” Bohince admits, floating through “tipsy polka,” rhubarb, wild carrot. There’s humor, too, and the promise of new beginnings: when a friend breastfeeds a newborn, the speaker coos at it in Gaelic.But the poet is at her recollective best when she allows herself a certain breadth to say things at length instead of condensing. A lot in _A Violence_ is as thick as Campbell’s soup:
> Was a swell commandant: drink up, sleep. She’d   
>   
> relinquished the vampy black and absconded to her toddler  
>   
> color _(muddy sunset)_ as we, one from each grief stage,   
>   
> commissioned to flock her, petal’d her pale strapless,  
>   
> pressed the appliqué along her spine with dancer’s glue,   
>   
> all funds sunk into that silk, hence the wan hors d’oeuvres,  
>   
> sheepish flasks, _White Album_ on a loop.
While the weeping in _A Violence_ may be copious (“then the world ordered _Weep_, and I wept”), one discovers there is no end to experience, scavenged from the macabre and quotidian in equal measure. Even simulacra can instruct, like a gold-plated earring tarnished “from its season in Hell” or when flakes land unfeelingly on the iris of a taxidermied deer. Bohince’s tender, Lowellian blend of family lore and remembrance comes together in “The Skunk,” a poem about her late mother, with stunning pathos:

## A Violence
> I went wild,  
>   
> memorizing her the way others did _Ozymandias_.  
>   
>   
> One Christmas, when I was grown, I wanted to cook for her  
>   
> the meal of a lifetime. To say, _Mom, This is living. This is love._ _Feel it._ Flakes of salt on closed lips of asparagus,  
>   
> duck limp-necked on a secondhand platter.  
>   
>   
> She kept her head down and ate fast, with shame, and gave me  
>   
> before leaving melted together wedding rings,  
>   
> hers and my dad’s. Amulet for I don’t know what.  
>   
> Pain-medallion. Coin for the underworld.  
>   
>   
> In the New Year, I flattened beneath  
>   
> the dentist’s lead apron and thought of her (I’m always  
>   
> thinking of her), her red pilled sweater, how she looked around  
>   
> at the candles, her face scorched from crying.
Like Proteus “in a high-up cave,” Bohince seems to carry within her a range of avatars, from “shirtless carpenters . . . on their summer jobs, / oiled as horses,” to Diego Velázquez and named lambs. Except, despite an homaging parenthetical to Elizabeth Bishop, Bohince more often resembles a less ornate version of Gjertrud Schnackenberg, whose gilded touch occasionally treats a beloved memory as grandparents used to a pair of baby’s shoes. Still, it’s undeniable that Bohince has a knack for writing disaster. Trying to mollify “the past, whatever that is,” she has been grieving in reverse, sketching whatever’s left of yesteryear in a manner that, however nostalgia-tinged, is mostly stoical—meaning “lighter, rinsed of those associations” which mattered profoundly once upon a time.

Title: 5 Book Reviews You Need to Read This Week

Our feast of fabulous reviews this week includes Niela Orr on Colson Whitehead’s _Cool Machine_, Lily Meyer on Valeria Luiselli’s _Beginning Middle End_, Jonathan Derbyshire on Emily Eakin’s _The Frenchme_ n, Jamie Quatro on Emilee Hackney’s _All That’s Unseen_, and Meghan Racklin on Emily Labarge’s _Dog Days_.
Brought to you byBook Marks, Lit Hub’s home for book reviews.
*
“At the start, he deployed humor as a cudgel against sentimentality or contrivance, but in recent years, he’s relented to sincerity, embracing deep feeling and even tenderness. Whitehead tends to use familiar narrative mechanisms (especially those belonging to genres like noir, horror, crime, and adventure) to chart unforeseen sensations or realities. He takes tropes and uses them to rope-a-dope the reader; he springs the traps laid by convention and the strictures of form in order to dictate his own course, to establish new norms. In particular, Whitehead repurposes ready-made narratives to explore underrepresented areas of Black experience; he consistently commits to the bit and then twists it, finding emotional resonances where you’d least expect them.
…
“_Cool Machine_, out tomorrow, is the final novel in his _Harlem Trilogy_, and it seems to take the spirit of that sixth writing rule about leaving things unsaid seriously. Along the way, Whitehead celebrates, in deliberately unsentimental fashion, the variety of Black ingenuity and splendor on offer in marginalized circles.
…

“In place of standardized hardboiled crime fiction, with its emphasis on formula and procedure,_Cool Machine_ is a sophisticated meditation on Black masculinity, aging, and unsanctioned political resistance (Du Bois defines crime as ‘the open rebellion of an individual against his social environment,’ which could apply to revolutionaries or gangsters). Rather than standard thievery, this novel considers another kind of seizure—what it means to lose time, and thus the potential to change, even as everything around you is being constantly reframed. Witnessing their development is the gift of getting to know characters on layaway over nine easy installments. But the insurance afforded by a series can also expose its inherent flaws. As in the first two novels, Carney and Pepper are put through the wringer, but I never felt like they were truly in trouble. The tropes of the crime novel wear thin, with its grim foreshadowing and prodigious exposition. The three-novella structure is sometimes predictable, with its movie-of-the-week rhythm, which requires resolution every hundred pages or so. But these are misdemeanors, easy to overlook.
…
“Although it’s a novel, I’m beginning to think of _Cool Machine_ as a counterhistory of Harlem’s underworld, one that surprises because it prioritizes human frailty and imagination. Regarding the fate of one mislaid item on the move in this final novel, we learn that there is a crucial two-week period that goes unaccounted for between what happens to the object and the revelation of its fate. The mystery of what exactly occurs in the interim belongs to one character alone—not even the reader knows what went down with real detail, though we can imagine. Here, Whitehead’s joking writing instruction comes in handy. Indeed, what isn’t said is important. In this case, some of the really good stuff happens off the page, in the minds of readers and in the hearts of rogue personalities we can’t quite pin down.”
–Niela Orr on Colson Whitehead’s**_Cool Machine_**(_Vulture_)

“But for those alarmed by the turbulence of midlife, the writer Valeria Luiselli’s novels offer a refreshingly different perspective. ‘I once read in a book by Saul Bellow that the difference between being alive and dead is just a matter of viewpoint,’ the narrator of Luiselli’s debut novel,_Faces in the Crowd_, recalls. She goes on to explain that the ‘living look from the center outward, the dead from the periphery to some kind of center.’ According to this worldview, the middle of life, far from a time to reset yourself, is the crux of human existence. And in Luiselli’s new novel,_Beginning Middle End_, it’s also where the messiest, most interesting, and most exciting parts of a story occur.
…
“Luiselli has long been intrigued by literary boredom._Beginning Middle End_, like all of her novels, goes without what its protagonist calls the ‘corset of plot.’ By no means does it lack drama—see: impending lover, maybe-sick mother; because this is Sicily, there’s also a looming volcano—but traditional story does not drive the novel forward. As it winds down, Luiselli does not resolve any of its questions (Is the mom all right? Will the narrator be able to write again?) but instead hands the narrative from the protagonist to her daughter. The novel’s final section takes on the daughter’s voice, and in its last lines, the daughter arbitrarily declares her mother’s book over: ‘This is the story,’ she says. ‘It has a beginning, a middle, and an end, and this is the end.’ By rejecting the myth of beginning again and the idea that endings are inherently meaningful, Luiselli highlights the fascination of the middle.
It’s a bold approach to life, more than literature. In the traditional arc of a book, of course, the ending can come only once. A beginning, meanwhile, sets a story’s tone and stakes. It tells the audience whom and what to care about, and creates, ideally, a sense of expectation and intrigue. Beginnings, in short, exist to make you want to read middles. In life, this can be tougher to accept; it’s hard to be in the middle, twisting between life and death.

Still, as my grandfather used to say, it beats the alternative. He was talking about dying, but also, I wouldn’t want to be (or have) a newborn forever, or ditch my husband after the honeymoon, or quit my job as soon as a challenge arises. Forging onward can sound duller and bleaker than launching a new life—hence, I think, the appeal of stories about multiverses—but in fact, it leads directly to the interesting stuff._Beginning Middle End_ knows that the first and last words in its title are just necessities. It’s the center, where life flails on, that counts.
–Lily Meyer on Valeria Luiselli’s_**Beginning Middle End**_(_The Atlantic_)
“…for students like Eakin, ‘deconstructing’ the fundamental assumptions of western metaphysics was heady stuff, even if you had only a ‘glancing familiarity’ with the great works of the philosophical tradition. So why, having fallen so comprehensively for theory, did she come to regard it as a ‘dangerous substance’ to be renounced or forsworn?
_The Frenchmen_ attempts to answer this question. And in doing so invites us to see Eakin’s own story as somehow symptomatic of the experience of what the critic Nicholas Dames has called the ‘Theory Generation.’ (It is ironic, incidentally, that this cohort should have seen its college years frequently depicted in a form—the realist novel—that theory did so much to ‘denaturalize and demystify,’ as Dames puts it. Think of books such as Jeffrey Eugenides’_The Marriage Plot_, Jonathan Franzen’s _The Corrections_ or Lorrie Moore’s _A Gate at the Stairs_.)

Title: An Aging Rake, An Ingenue, And A Strapping Young Painter In 'Tristana'
Chunks: 0,1
###### Tristana
By Benito Perez Galdos, Margaret Jull Costa
History and literature are fraught with men of insatiable appetites, who use their gifts of seduction to charm their way into many a bedroom: Casanova, Lord Byron, Don Juan, the list goes on. In _Tristana_, Benito Pérez Galdós' masterful 1892 novel — newly reissued by NYRB Classics in a translation by Margaret Jull Costa — we meet a man of Byronic decadence: Don Lope, an aging lover whose sexual conquests know no bounds. He's a man of contradictory ideals, who's developed a complex and manufactured morality that lets him prey on the unfortunate while still maintaining a sense of himself as a gentleman. Poetry and philosophy at its crux, the novel is a bold and telling illustration of 19th century Spain.
The Tristana of the title is a beautiful orphan whose family debts have been paid by the dubiously gallant Don Lope. Before long, he falls for her, and applies, as he puts it, "the law of love." Three times Tristana's age, the old wretch takes her captive and makes her his property; Tristana, not knowing any better, puts up with it.
Eventually, though, she comes to her senses, and in her intimate conversations with the house maid Saturna, Tristana begins to voice her desire to be free, to be the property of no man. Perhaps she'll write, paint, learn other languages. In her mind, the possibilities are truly endless — and when she meets the young, strapping painter Horacio, everything changes. Having never been so taken aback by anyone, she pleads with Saturna to steer her right: "Advise me, guide me. I don't know about these things." Tristana and Horacio, enamored of one another, soon begin exchanging letters and meeting for walks.
Don Lope suspects that Tristana is seeing someone, which she denies profusely. When — after much interrogation — she finally comes clean concerning her relationship with Horacio, their lives take on a new rhythm. But then Tristana falls gravely ill, the prospect of happiness becomes more of an illusion, and desperate choices must be made.

###### Tristana
Pérez Galdós has long been revered as one of the greatest European novelists, and _Tristana_ leaves us with little doubt as to why. His treatment of Don Lope is a testament to his overwhelming ability as an architect of characters: While he establishes early on that the old predator operates out of a fairly illogical moral center, he doesn't neglect Don Lope's innate sense of charity and altruism — a certain goodness that makes it more difficult to dismiss the man completely. Pérez Galdós leaves it up to the reader to decide just what to make of Don Lope and his predilections. Is he an entirely bad person? Are any of us righteous enough to judge him?
Even more interesting is the way Pérez Galdós writes about women, with veiled rants about their mistreatment that border on modern feminism. His description of Tristana's mental enslavement is stunning, making much of the sheer wrongness without getting preachy. Though not overtly political, Pérez Galdós offers a glimpse at the limitations placed on women in an era when opportunities were scarce and the injustices were plenty.
Told in sophisticated yet enveloping prose, _Tristana_ is a treasure that should not be overlooked. Pérez Galdós barely breaks a sweat as he weaves a tale of intelligence and emotional richness comparable to the works of Charles Dickens and Gustave Flaubert. And while the pace of the story is expertly controlled, there is an urgency to each sentence, paragraph, page. At its heart, it's about how we should hurry up and become who we are. Or else.
_Juan Vidal is a writer and critic for_ NPR Books _. He's on Twitter: @itsjuanlove_ _._

The Goldfinch by Carel Fabritius
The Road by Cormac McCarthy and Middlesex by Jeffery Eugenides are two of the great American novels of the 21st Century. Both won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction; to that brace you can now add The Goldfinch by Donna Tartt. It picked up the prize this year and, oh, how richly deserved it is.
In comparative terms it is closer to Eugenides’ masterpiece than McCarthy’s stripped down telling of The Road. Like Middlesex this a story that broadly sweeps over time and must be considered one of the ‘Great American Novels’.
Whilst storytelling is at the very core of this magnificent novel, characterisation and profound messaging are vital cogs in its success.
It concerns the first 30 or so years of the life of Theo Decker, a young boy who has his first love, his mother, tragically torn away from him in a terrorist (we assume) bombing of an American Museum (the Met we assume) when he was a kid. In the process Theo grabs from the ruins a canvas that has been freed from its frame as a result of the explosion. The canvas (a board actually) is a painting of a captive Goldfinch. Small, unpretentious, delicate but delightful and considered a true masterpiece by famed (but obscure) 17th Century Dutch painter Carel Fabritius.
His new found ‘ownership’ is to underscore the remainder of Theodore Decker’s life.
What follows is as engrossing a tale as you’ll ever read. It tells Decker’s life, told throughout in the first person, in a series of extended chapters. Each one dealing with an episode in his existence that is forever uncertain riding it out, as he does, on an absurdly thin line between happiness and chaos.
Although he has a father, he is estranged and only enters the story a quarter of the way in. By then we have established a complex character in Theo and his geeky school friend, Andy, Andy’s family who ‘adopt’ him as he has nowhere to go and his,frankly bonkers,Ukranian school mate, Boris, who becomes a central character in the novel.

But aside from Theo and Boris the two main protagonists are his deceased mother (who suffuses everything Theo does in life) and The Goldfinch. This chained bird is a metaphor for Theo’s life. As, like the bird, he is imprisoned by fate and can’t ever really find true happiness.
His love life is, to say the least, complicated and utterly unfulfilling. I won’t spoil it by revealing the complexities of his relationships but suffice it to say they form a key subplot in the tale.
What Donna Tartt does (always does) is craft a fine plot but then weave it together with extraordinary depth of descriptive prose and utterly believable characterisation and dialogue; although huge swathes of the book are dialogue-free, as we get to grips with how Theo is feeling about the latest episode he finds himself in. Yet the book clips along at a rate of knots that keeps you wanting more and more – that’s some feat for a novel of 864 pages. (Donna Tartt may not be prolific but each of her novels is two or three of anyone else’s.)
This is a book fundamentally about love and the nature of good and evil. One might imagine Boris on one shoulder horned and trident-bearing; Polly, Hobie and Theo’s mother on the other festooned in white.
And Theo is torn.
The grief that suffuses his whole being at the loss of his beloved (no, truly adored) mother never leaves the book and it’s only Boris’ honest, frank joie de vivre and adherence to his own highly unorthodox rule book for life that adds sparkle and happiness, of a sort, to the young Theo’s life: the drink and drugs help too, but they are merely a cushion for Theo’s profound grieving.
This novel is a rare and precious thing. A story that is almost without blemish. A thing of startling beauty and an absolute must read for anyone who ever enjoyed the art of storytelling; because here it is in all its wonder.
This is a masterclass in writing that stands shoulder to shoulder with the greatest storytelling that America has ever produced.
The movie could, and should, be epic. My money’s on David Fincher (no pun intended) directing it and sweeping the boards at the Oscars.
the view from the very, very back row of the upper circle of the Usher hall
Oh my Lord.

You know when bands hire six cello players to play on TV programmes like Later…with Jools Holland and it’s quite good? Adds a wee frisson?
Well try touring with your six piece band and a 26 piece (est.) orchestra. Now, that’s more than a frisson, that’s a full blown “When Harry Met Sally” moment.
Actually much more than a moment. This was two hours of ecstasy in a world class acoustic venue.
I saw John Grant on the Park Stage at Glastonbury this year and he was my joint favourite act (alongside Massive Attack) but that was rock and roll/clubland electronica. This was very different.
He has enlisted the help of Fiona Bryce to score his first two albums and at least four new songs and jeepers, the results really are quite remarkable.
In particular the Wagneresque (although I think he claimed it was Rachmaninov) opening to Pale Green Ghosts that literally blew the audience away.Glacier was truly astonishing.
Contrast that with “_But I am the greatest motherfucker that you’re ever gonna meet from the top of my head down to the tips of my toes on my feet_” and you get the measure of the man. He’s electrifying.
He’s also humble.
It was a rare treat tonight and I feel honoured to have shared a night with him.
I am a cinephile.
I can easily do difficult movies. Under The Skin. The White Ribbon. Cache. Jeez I can do all the tough stuff.
I am a Mike Leigh-phile too.
Secrets and Lies, Naked, Life is Sweet, Abigail’;s Party, Nuts in May. All brilliant.
I am a Timothy Spall-phile also. (Just too many to mention)
And so I approached Mr Turner with gusto. I like Turner’s seascapes very much. What is there not to like?
It turns out, quite a lot.
To cut to the chase this is one of the dullest 2.5 hours I have spent in a cinema in many a long year. Turgid, plotless, meandering, self-indulgent claptrap of the highest order.
The cinematography has its moments but it takes a lot of moments to make a movie.

There are scenes that are enjoyable, largely in the Royal Academy and one in particular when Constable is ridiculed by Turner but overall it is a study in very dull misogyny that the world is probably no worse without.
Perhaps the most interesting aspect of this movie was the development of his supposed housekeeper Hannah Dandy’s (Dorothy Atkinson) eczema. Was she, or was she not, Turner’s wife/mistress/muse?
Who cares.
Turner-phile ladies sat behind me in the audience and whispered throughout. Damn them.
Utter shite.
Mike Leigh’s worst film by a country mile.
The British Government essentially killed Alan Turing.
The man who invented what we now consider the ‘computer’ and he may have saved 14 million people from death because of his contribution, sorry vast contribution, to the foreshortening of the Second World War through his invention of the Enigma code breaking machine. Churchill thought so.
But, the trouble is, you see, Alan Turing was a homosexual. And the British Government (like many governments today) did not like homosexuals.
Homosexuals in the post war years were lepers of society. So the British Government chemically castrated him. (Better than going to prison for touching a man’s penis? Your call.)
Alan Turing was most likely also a sufferer of Aspergers Syndrome.
He was, in every sense of the word, a genius.
He was not a likeable man because to make real, substantial change sometimes eschews popularity. He was not popular.
It’s a dream role for an actor of substance. That actor is Benedict Cumberbatch.
At the time of writing Cumberbatch has seven movies in production, new episodes of the BBC’s Sherlock and a couple of episodes of The Hollow Crown as Richard III as work in progress. It would seem reasonable to assume from this that he is a man in demand.
Why?
Because he is a brilliant actor. And this is his time. This is most certainly his movie. Yes, he has good support from Keira Knightley, Allen Leech, Matthew Goode and especially Mark Strong, as his ‘boss’. Charles Dance moves on from his movie idol roles into the baddie spotlight and carries it off effortlessly. But make no mistake. This is ALL about Benedict Cumberbatch.
Biopics are often easy meat because they can be imitation games.

# Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes
November 29, 2014 November 29, 2014
Reading _Don Quixote_ has been a year-long project for me in 2014. After reading _Clarissa_ over a twelve month period as part of a readalong in 2012 and then _War and Peace_ in 2013 I decided to tackle another of the very long, intimidating classics on my Classics Club list, this time on my own. Now that I’ve finished I don’t know why I had ever been intimidated by it. Yes, it’s long (over 1,000 pages in most editions) and old (originally published in two parts in 1605 and 1615) and a translation, but I didn’t find it difficult to read at all. It’s fun and imaginative and entertaining – and I loved it.
_Don Quixote_ is the story of a gentleman of La Mancha who has spent so many years reading books of chivalry and romance that he has come to believe the tales they tell are true. Inspired by the heroes of his favourite books, he decides to become a knight errant and go out into the world in search of adventures. Renaming himself Don Quixote and his horse Rocinante, he convinces a neighbouring peasant, Sancho Panza, to join him as his squire. With Sancho at his side, Don Quixote sets out to right wrongs, fight duels and rescue damsels in distress, in the hope that his valiant deeds will win him the love of the beautiful (and largely imaginary) Dulcinea del Toboso.
As Don Quixote and Sancho travel across Spain they have one adventure after another, each one headed with a long and intriguing chapter title such as _“Of the strange adventure which befell the valiant Don Quixote with the bold Knight of the Mirrors”_ or _“Which deals with the adventure of the enchanted head, together with other trivial matters which cannot be left untold”_. As you read on, however, it soon becomes obvious that these ‘adventures’ are not quite as amazing as they sound and usually have a logical explanation.

# Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes
Many people, even without reading the book, will have heard of the famous ‘tilting at windmills’ episode. There are many, many other similar episodes in the novel but this one appears near the beginning which is probably why it’s the best known. If you’re not familiar with it, on approaching some windmills in a field Don Quixote becomes convinced they are giants and attacks them with his sword:
> “What giants?” said Sancho Panza.  
>   
>   
> “Those thou seest there,” answered his master, “with the long arms, and some have them nearly two leagues long.”  
>   
>   
> “Look, your worship,” said Sancho; “what we see there are not giants but windmills, and what seem to be their arms are the sails that, turned by the wind, make the millstone go.”  
>   
>   
> “It is easy to see,” replied Don Quixote, “that thou art not used to this business of adventures; those are giants; and if thou art afraid, away with thee out of this and betake thyself to prayer while I engage them in fierce and unequal combat.”
This is a pattern that is repeated over and over again throughout the novel: Don Quixote mistakes inns for castles and flocks of sheep for armies – and even when Sancho points out the truth he still insists that he is right. The castles and the armies must have been enchanted by great wizards, he says, so that they appear to be inns and sheep. As the story progresses, Don Quixote’s fame spreads and he is thought of as insane and Sancho as an idiot. The response of some of the people they meet can be very cruel and it’s quite sad to see how Don Quixote and Sancho are ridiculed, scorned and made the target of elaborate practical jokes. I wouldn’t describe this as a sad book, though; in fact, it’s a very funny one. The humour doesn’t always work (being four hundred years old and in translation, maybe that’s not surprising) but at times it’s hilarious!

# Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes
As well as the adventures and the humour, there are lots of songs, poems and ballads interspersed with the prose. There are also lots of stories-within-stories – almost everyone they meet on their journey has a long and tragic story of their own to tell – and many of these have no relevance to the rest of the novel. For example, a lot of time is devoted to the tale of a Christian who was held captive by Moors in Algiers and has escaped back to Spain – nothing to do with Don Quixote, but apparently based on Cervantes’ own experiences. This is why the novel is so long and why you need to have some patience with it! Reading this book over a period of several months was the perfect strategy for me as the episodic nature of the story meant that I could leave it for a few weeks and still get straight back into it when I picked it up again. Breaking it up into small sections kept it feeling fresh and interesting so that I never felt bored or overwhelmed.
A quick note on the translation now. There have been many English translations of _Don Quixote_ over the years but not really having any idea which to choose, I started reading the 1885 John Ormsby translation (in the public domain so free to download from Project Gutenberg and other websites) and I found it perfectly readable so decided just to stick with it. I wouldn’t necessarily recommend that translation to everyone as it does use some archaic terms and feels ‘old’ but that’s what I prefer when I’m reading an old book so it wasn’t a problem for me. Whichever may be closest to the literal translation, Ormsby’s description of Don Quixote as “Knight of the Rueful Countenance” just sounds better to me than, for example, Edith Grossman’s “Knight of the Sorrowful Face”. It’s a matter of personal taste, though, so it’s probably a good idea to look at a few different translations and find one that suits you before you embark on such a long novel!
Much as I enjoyed this book it did sometimes feel as if I was never going to finish it, so I was pleased to reach the end. I’m going to miss Don Quixote and Sancho, though, after spending so much time with them this year!

###### Tristana
By Benito Perez Galdos, Margaret Jull Costa
History and literature are fraught with men of insatiable appetites, who use their gifts of seduction to charm their way into many a bedroom: Casanova, Lord Byron, Don Juan, the list goes on. In _Tristana_, Benito Pérez Galdós' masterful 1892 novel — newly reissued by NYRB Classics in a translation by Margaret Jull Costa — we meet a man of Byronic decadence: Don Lope, an aging lover whose sexual conquests know no bounds. He's a man of contradictory ideals, who's developed a complex and manufactured morality that lets him prey on the unfortunate while still maintaining a sense of himself as a gentleman. Poetry and philosophy at its crux, the novel is a bold and telling illustration of 19th century Spain.
The Tristana of the title is a beautiful orphan whose family debts have been paid by the dubiously gallant Don Lope. Before long, he falls for her, and applies, as he puts it, "the law of love." Three times Tristana's age, the old wretch takes her captive and makes her his property; Tristana, not knowing any better, puts up with it.
Eventually, though, she comes to her senses, and in her intimate conversations with the house maid Saturna, Tristana begins to voice her desire to be free, to be the property of no man. Perhaps she'll write, paint, learn other languages. In her mind, the possibilities are truly endless — and when she meets the young, strapping painter Horacio, everything changes. Having never been so taken aback by anyone, she pleads with Saturna to steer her right: "Advise me, guide me. I don't know about these things." Tristana and Horacio, enamored of one another, soon begin exchanging letters and meeting for walks.
Don Lope suspects that Tristana is seeing someone, which she denies profusely. When — after much interrogation — she finally comes clean concerning her relationship with Horacio, their lives take on a new rhythm. But then Tristana falls gravely ill, the prospect of happiness becomes more of an illusion, and desperate choices must be made.
texts.1:
###### Tristana
Pérez Galdós has long been revered as one of the greatest European novelists, and _Tristana_ leaves us with little doubt as to why. His treatment of Don Lope is a testament to his overwhelming ability as an architect of characters: While he establishes early on that the old predator operates out of a fairly illogical moral center, he doesn't neglect Don Lope's innate sense of charity and altruism — a certain goodness that makes it more difficult to dismiss the man completely. Pérez Galdós leaves it up to the reader to decide just what to make of Don Lope and his predilections. Is he an entirely bad person? Are any of us righteous enough to judge him?
Even more interesting is the way Pérez Galdós writes about women, with veiled rants about their mistreatment that border on modern feminism. His description of Tristana's mental enslavement is stunning, making much of the sheer wrongness without getting preachy. Though not overtly political, Pérez Galdós offers a glimpse at the limitations placed on women in an era when opportunities were scarce and the injustices were plenty.
Told in sophisticated yet enveloping prose, _Tristana_ is a treasure that should not be overlooked. Pérez Galdós barely breaks a sweat as he weaves a tale of intelligence and emotional richness comparable to the works of Charles Dickens and Gustave Flaubert. And while the pace of the story is expertly controlled, there is an urgency to each sentence, paragraph, page. At its heart, it's about how we should hurry up and become who we are. Or else.
_Juan Vidal is a writer and critic for_ NPR Books _. He's on Twitter: @itsjuanlove_ _._

The Goldfinch by Carel Fabritius
The Road by Cormac McCarthy and Middlesex by Jeffery Eugenides are two of the great American novels of the 21st Century. Both won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction; to that brace you can now add The Goldfinch by Donna Tartt. It picked up the prize this year and, oh, how richly deserved it is.
In comparative terms it is closer to Eugenides’ masterpiece than McCarthy’s stripped down telling of The Road. Like Middlesex this a story that broadly sweeps over time and must be considered one of the ‘Great American Novels’.
Whilst storytelling is at the very core of this magnificent novel, characterisation and profound messaging are vital cogs in its success.
It concerns the first 30 or so years of the life of Theo Decker, a young boy who has his first love, his mother, tragically torn away from him in a terrorist (we assume) bombing of an American Museum (the Met we assume) when he was a kid. In the process Theo grabs from the ruins a canvas that has been freed from its frame as a result of the explosion. The canvas (a board actually) is a painting of a captive Goldfinch. Small, unpretentious, delicate but delightful and considered a true masterpiece by famed (but obscure) 17th Century Dutch painter Carel Fabritius.
His new found ‘ownership’ is to underscore the remainder of Theodore Decker’s life.
What follows is as engrossing a tale as you’ll ever read. It tells Decker’s life, told throughout in the first person, in a series of extended chapters. Each one dealing with an episode in his existence that is forever uncertain riding it out, as he does, on an absurdly thin line between happiness and chaos.
Although he has a father, he is estranged and only enters the story a quarter of the way in. By then we have established a complex character in Theo and his geeky school friend, Andy, Andy’s family who ‘adopt’ him as he has nowhere to go and his,frankly bonkers,Ukranian school mate, Boris, who becomes a central character in the novel.
texts.1:
But aside from Theo and Boris the two main protagonists are his deceased mother (who suffuses everything Theo does in life) and The Goldfinch. This chained bird is a metaphor for Theo’s life. As, like the bird, he is imprisoned by fate and can’t ever really find true happiness.
His love life is, to say the least, complicated and utterly unfulfilling. I won’t spoil it by revealing the complexities of his relationships but suffice it to say they form a key subplot in the tale.
What Donna Tartt does (always does) is craft a fine plot but then weave it together with extraordinary depth of descriptive prose and utterly believable characterisation and dialogue; although huge swathes of the book are dialogue-free, as we get to grips with how Theo is feeling about the latest episode he finds himself in. Yet the book clips along at a rate of knots that keeps you wanting more and more – that’s some feat for a novel of 864 pages. (Donna Tartt may not be prolific but each of her novels is two or three of anyone else’s.)
This is a book fundamentally about love and the nature of good and evil. One might imagine Boris on one shoulder horned and trident-bearing; Polly, Hobie and Theo’s mother on the other festooned in white.
And Theo is torn.
The grief that suffuses his whole being at the loss of his beloved (no, truly adored) mother never leaves the book and it’s only Boris’ honest, frank joie de vivre and adherence to his own highly unorthodox rule book for life that adds sparkle and happiness, of a sort, to the young Theo’s life: the drink and drugs help too, but they are merely a cushion for Theo’s profound grieving.
This novel is a rare and precious thing. A story that is almost without blemish. A thing of startling beauty and an absolute must read for anyone who ever enjoyed the art of storytelling; because here it is in all its wonder.
This is a masterclass in writing that stands shoulder to shoulder with the greatest storytelling that America has ever produced.
The movie could, and should, be epic. My money’s on David Fincher (no pun intended) directing it and sweeping the boards at the Oscars.
the view from the very, very back row of the upper circle of the Usher hall
Oh my Lord.
texts.2:
You know when bands hire six cello players to play on TV programmes like Later…with Jools Holland and it’s quite good? Adds a wee frisson?
Well try touring with your six piece band and a 26 piece (est.) orchestra. Now, that’s more than a frisson, that’s a full blown “When Harry Met Sally” moment.
Actually much more than a moment. This was two hours of ecstasy in a world class acoustic venue.
I saw John Grant on the Park Stage at Glastonbury this year and he was my joint favourite act (alongside Massive Attack) but that was rock and roll/clubland electronica. This was very different.
He has enlisted the help of Fiona Bryce to score his first two albums and at least four new songs and jeepers, the results really are quite remarkable.
In particular the Wagneresque (although I think he claimed it was Rachmaninov) opening to Pale Green Ghosts that literally blew the audience away.Glacier was truly astonishing.
Contrast that with “_But I am the greatest motherfucker that you’re ever gonna meet from the top of my head down to the tips of my toes on my feet_” and you get the measure of the man. He’s electrifying.
He’s also humble.
It was a rare treat tonight and I feel honoured to have shared a night with him.
I am a cinephile.
I can easily do difficult movies. Under The Skin. The White Ribbon. Cache. Jeez I can do all the tough stuff.
I am a Mike Leigh-phile too.
Secrets and Lies, Naked, Life is Sweet, Abigail’;s Party, Nuts in May. All brilliant.
I am a Timothy Spall-phile also. (Just too many to mention)
And so I approached Mr Turner with gusto. I like Turner’s seascapes very much. What is there not to like?
It turns out, quite a lot.
To cut to the chase this is one of the dullest 2.5 hours I have spent in a cinema in many a long year. Turgid, plotless, meandering, self-indulgent claptrap of the highest order.
The cinematography has its moments but it takes a lot of moments to make a movie.
texts.3:
There are scenes that are enjoyable, largely in the Royal Academy and one in particular when Constable is ridiculed by Turner but overall it is a study in very dull misogyny that the world is probably no worse without.
Perhaps the most interesting aspect of this movie was the development of his supposed housekeeper Hannah Dandy’s (Dorothy Atkinson) eczema. Was she, or was she not, Turner’s wife/mistress/muse?
Who cares.
Turner-phile ladies sat behind me in the audience and whispered throughout. Damn them.
Utter shite.
Mike Leigh’s worst film by a country mile.
The British Government essentially killed Alan Turing.
The man who invented what we now consider the ‘computer’ and he may have saved 14 million people from death because of his contribution, sorry vast contribution, to the foreshortening of the Second World War through his invention of the Enigma code breaking machine. Churchill thought so.
But, the trouble is, you see, Alan Turing was a homosexual. And the British Government (like many governments today) did not like homosexuals.
Homosexuals in the post war years were lepers of society. So the British Government chemically castrated him. (Better than going to prison for touching a man’s penis? Your call.)
Alan Turing was most likely also a sufferer of Aspergers Syndrome.
He was, in every sense of the word, a genius.
He was not a likeable man because to make real, substantial change sometimes eschews popularity. He was not popular.
It’s a dream role for an actor of substance. That actor is Benedict Cumberbatch.
At the time of writing Cumberbatch has seven movies in production, new episodes of the BBC’s Sherlock and a couple of episodes of The Hollow Crown as Richard III as work in progress. It would seem reasonable to assume from this that he is a man in demand.
Why?
Because he is a brilliant actor. And this is his time. This is most certainly his movie. Yes, he has good support from Keira Knightley, Allen Leech, Matthew Goode and especially Mark Strong, as his ‘boss’. Charles Dance moves on from his movie idol roles into the baddie spotlight and carries it off effortlessly. But make no mistake. This is ALL about Benedict Cumberbatch.
Biopics are often easy meat because they can be imitation games.

# Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes
November 29, 2014 November 29, 2014
Reading _Don Quixote_ has been a year-long project for me in 2014. After reading _Clarissa_ over a twelve month period as part of a readalong in 2012 and then _War and Peace_ in 2013 I decided to tackle another of the very long, intimidating classics on my Classics Club list, this time on my own. Now that I’ve finished I don’t know why I had ever been intimidated by it. Yes, it’s long (over 1,000 pages in most editions) and old (originally published in two parts in 1605 and 1615) and a translation, but I didn’t find it difficult to read at all. It’s fun and imaginative and entertaining – and I loved it.
_Don Quixote_ is the story of a gentleman of La Mancha who has spent so many years reading books of chivalry and romance that he has come to believe the tales they tell are true. Inspired by the heroes of his favourite books, he decides to become a knight errant and go out into the world in search of adventures. Renaming himself Don Quixote and his horse Rocinante, he convinces a neighbouring peasant, Sancho Panza, to join him as his squire. With Sancho at his side, Don Quixote sets out to right wrongs, fight duels and rescue damsels in distress, in the hope that his valiant deeds will win him the love of the beautiful (and largely imaginary) Dulcinea del Toboso.
As Don Quixote and Sancho travel across Spain they have one adventure after another, each one headed with a long and intriguing chapter title such as _“Of the strange adventure which befell the valiant Don Quixote with the bold Knight of the Mirrors”_ or _“Which deals with the adventure of the enchanted head, together with other trivial matters which cannot be left untold”_. As you read on, however, it soon becomes obvious that these ‘adventures’ are not quite as amazing as they sound and usually have a logical explanation.

# Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes
Many people, even without reading the book, will have heard of the famous ‘tilting at windmills’ episode. There are many, many other similar episodes in the novel but this one appears near the beginning which is probably why it’s the best known. If you’re not familiar with it, on approaching some windmills in a field Don Quixote becomes convinced they are giants and attacks them with his sword:
> “What giants?” said Sancho Panza.  
>   
>   
> “Those thou seest there,” answered his master, “with the long arms, and some have them nearly two leagues long.”  
>   
>   
> “Look, your worship,” said Sancho; “what we see there are not giants but windmills, and what seem to be their arms are the sails that, turned by the wind, make the millstone go.”  
>   
>   
> “It is easy to see,” replied Don Quixote, “that thou art not used to this business of adventures; those are giants; and if thou art afraid, away with thee out of this and betake thyself to prayer while I engage them in fierce and unequal combat.”
This is a pattern that is repeated over and over again throughout the novel: Don Quixote mistakes inns for castles and flocks of sheep for armies – and even when Sancho points out the truth he still insists that he is right. The castles and the armies must have been enchanted by great wizards, he says, so that they appear to be inns and sheep. As the story progresses, Don Quixote’s fame spreads and he is thought of as insane and Sancho as an idiot. The response of some of the people they meet can be very cruel and it’s quite sad to see how Don Quixote and Sancho are ridiculed, scorned and made the target of elaborate practical jokes. I wouldn’t describe this as a sad book, though; in fact, it’s a very funny one. The humour doesn’t always work (being four hundred years old and in translation, maybe that’s not surprising) but at times it’s hilarious!
texts.5:
# Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes
As well as the adventures and the humour, there are lots of songs, poems and ballads interspersed with the prose. There are also lots of stories-within-stories – almost everyone they meet on their journey has a long and tragic story of their own to tell – and many of these have no relevance to the rest of the novel. For example, a lot of time is devoted to the tale of a Christian who was held captive by Moors in Algiers and has escaped back to Spain – nothing to do with Don Quixote, but apparently based on Cervantes’ own experiences. This is why the novel is so long and why you need to have some patience with it! Reading this book over a period of several months was the perfect strategy for me as the episodic nature of the story meant that I could leave it for a few weeks and still get straight back into it when I picked it up again. Breaking it up into small sections kept it feeling fresh and interesting so that I never felt bored or overwhelmed.
A quick note on the translation now. There have been many English translations of _Don Quixote_ over the years but not really having any idea which to choose, I started reading the 1885 John Ormsby translation (in the public domain so free to download from Project Gutenberg and other websites) and I found it perfectly readable so decided just to stick with it. I wouldn’t necessarily recommend that translation to everyone as it does use some archaic terms and feels ‘old’ but that’s what I prefer when I’m reading an old book so it wasn’t a problem for me. Whichever may be closest to the literal translation, Ormsby’s description of Don Quixote as “Knight of the Rueful Countenance” just sounds better to me than, for example, Edith Grossman’s “Knight of the Sorrowful Face”. It’s a matter of personal taste, though, so it’s probably a good idea to look at a few different translations and find one that suits you before you embark on such a long novel!
Much as I enjoyed this book it did sometimes feel as if I was never going to finish it, so I was pleased to reach the end. I’m going to miss Don Quixote and Sancho, though, after spending so much time with them this year!

###### Tristana
By Benito Perez Galdos, Margaret Jull Costa
History and literature are fraught with men of insatiable appetites, who use their gifts of seduction to charm their way into many a bedroom: Casanova, Lord Byron, Don Juan, the list goes on. In _Tristana_, Benito Pérez Galdós' masterful 1892 novel — newly reissued by NYRB Classics in a translation by Margaret Jull Costa — we meet a man of Byronic decadence: Don Lope, an aging lover whose sexual conquests know no bounds. He's a man of contradictory ideals, who's developed a complex and manufactured morality that lets him prey on the unfortunate while still maintaining a sense of himself as a gentleman. Poetry and philosophy at its crux, the novel is a bold and telling illustration of 19th century Spain.
The Tristana of the title is a beautiful orphan whose family debts have been paid by the dubiously gallant Don Lope. Before long, he falls for her, and applies, as he puts it, "the law of love." Three times Tristana's age, the old wretch takes her captive and makes her his property; Tristana, not knowing any better, puts up with it.
Eventually, though, she comes to her senses, and in her intimate conversations with the house maid Saturna, Tristana begins to voice her desire to be free, to be the property of no man. Perhaps she'll write, paint, learn other languages. In her mind, the possibilities are truly endless — and when she meets the young, strapping painter Horacio, everything changes. Having never been so taken aback by anyone, she pleads with Saturna to steer her right: "Advise me, guide me. I don't know about these things." Tristana and Horacio, enamored of one another, soon begin exchanging letters and meeting for walks.
Don Lope suspects that Tristana is seeing someone, which she denies profusely. When — after much interrogation — she finally comes clean concerning her relationship with Horacio, their lives take on a new rhythm. But then Tristana falls gravely ill, the prospect of happiness becomes more of an illusion, and desperate choices must be made.

###### Tristana
Pérez Galdós has long been revered as one of the greatest European novelists, and _Tristana_ leaves us with little doubt as to why. His treatment of Don Lope is a testament to his overwhelming ability as an architect of characters: While he establishes early on that the old predator operates out of a fairly illogical moral center, he doesn't neglect Don Lope's innate sense of charity and altruism — a certain goodness that makes it more difficult to dismiss the man completely. Pérez Galdós leaves it up to the reader to decide just what to make of Don Lope and his predilections. Is he an entirely bad person? Are any of us righteous enough to judge him?
Even more interesting is the way Pérez Galdós writes about women, with veiled rants about their mistreatment that border on modern feminism. His description of Tristana's mental enslavement is stunning, making much of the sheer wrongness without getting preachy. Though not overtly political, Pérez Galdós offers a glimpse at the limitations placed on women in an era when opportunities were scarce and the injustices were plenty.
Told in sophisticated yet enveloping prose, _Tristana_ is a treasure that should not be overlooked. Pérez Galdós barely breaks a sweat as he weaves a tale of intelligence and emotional richness comparable to the works of Charles Dickens and Gustave Flaubert. And while the pace of the story is expertly controlled, there is an urgency to each sentence, paragraph, page. At its heart, it's about how we should hurry up and become who we are. Or else.
_Juan Vidal is a writer and critic for_ NPR Books _. He's on Twitter: @itsjuanlove_ _._
