The Goldfinch by Carel Fabritius
The Road by Cormac McCarthy and Middlesex by Jeffery Eugenides are two of the great American novels of the 21st Century. Both won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction; to that brace you can now add The Goldfinch by Donna Tartt. It picked up the prize this year and, oh, how richly deserved it is.
In comparative terms it is closer to Eugenides’ masterpiece than McCarthy’s stripped down telling of The Road. Like Middlesex this a story that broadly sweeps over time and must be considered one of the ‘Great American Novels’.
Whilst storytelling is at the very core of this magnificent novel, characterisation and profound messaging are vital cogs in its success.
It concerns the first 30 or so years of the life of Theo Decker, a young boy who has his first love, his mother, tragically torn away from him in a terrorist (we assume) bombing of an American Museum (the Met we assume) when he was a kid. In the process Theo grabs from the ruins a canvas that has been freed from its frame as a result of the explosion. The canvas (a board actually) is a painting of a captive Goldfinch. Small, unpretentious, delicate but delightful and considered a true masterpiece by famed (but obscure) 17th Century Dutch painter Carel Fabritius.
His new found ‘ownership’ is to underscore the remainder of Theodore Decker’s life.
What follows is as engrossing a tale as you’ll ever read. It tells Decker’s life, told throughout in the first person, in a series of extended chapters. Each one dealing with an episode in his existence that is forever uncertain riding it out, as he does, on an absurdly thin line between happiness and chaos.
Although he has a father, he is estranged and only enters the story a quarter of the way in. By then we have established a complex character in Theo and his geeky school friend, Andy, Andy’s family who ‘adopt’ him as he has nowhere to go and his,frankly bonkers,Ukranian school mate, Boris, who becomes a central character in the novel.

But aside from Theo and Boris the two main protagonists are his deceased mother (who suffuses everything Theo does in life) and The Goldfinch. This chained bird is a metaphor for Theo’s life. As, like the bird, he is imprisoned by fate and can’t ever really find true happiness.
His love life is, to say the least, complicated and utterly unfulfilling. I won’t spoil it by revealing the complexities of his relationships but suffice it to say they form a key subplot in the tale.
What Donna Tartt does (always does) is craft a fine plot but then weave it together with extraordinary depth of descriptive prose and utterly believable characterisation and dialogue; although huge swathes of the book are dialogue-free, as we get to grips with how Theo is feeling about the latest episode he finds himself in. Yet the book clips along at a rate of knots that keeps you wanting more and more – that’s some feat for a novel of 864 pages. (Donna Tartt may not be prolific but each of her novels is two or three of anyone else’s.)
This is a book fundamentally about love and the nature of good and evil. One might imagine Boris on one shoulder horned and trident-bearing; Polly, Hobie and Theo’s mother on the other festooned in white.
And Theo is torn.
The grief that suffuses his whole being at the loss of his beloved (no, truly adored) mother never leaves the book and it’s only Boris’ honest, frank joie de vivre and adherence to his own highly unorthodox rule book for life that adds sparkle and happiness, of a sort, to the young Theo’s life: the drink and drugs help too, but they are merely a cushion for Theo’s profound grieving.
This novel is a rare and precious thing. A story that is almost without blemish. A thing of startling beauty and an absolute must read for anyone who ever enjoyed the art of storytelling; because here it is in all its wonder.
This is a masterclass in writing that stands shoulder to shoulder with the greatest storytelling that America has ever produced.
The movie could, and should, be epic. My money’s on David Fincher (no pun intended) directing it and sweeping the boards at the Oscars.
the view from the very, very back row of the upper circle of the Usher hall
Oh my Lord.

You know when bands hire six cello players to play on TV programmes like Later…with Jools Holland and it’s quite good? Adds a wee frisson?
Well try touring with your six piece band and a 26 piece (est.) orchestra. Now, that’s more than a frisson, that’s a full blown “When Harry Met Sally” moment.
Actually much more than a moment. This was two hours of ecstasy in a world class acoustic venue.
I saw John Grant on the Park Stage at Glastonbury this year and he was my joint favourite act (alongside Massive Attack) but that was rock and roll/clubland electronica. This was very different.
He has enlisted the help of Fiona Bryce to score his first two albums and at least four new songs and jeepers, the results really are quite remarkable.
In particular the Wagneresque (although I think he claimed it was Rachmaninov) opening to Pale Green Ghosts that literally blew the audience away.Glacier was truly astonishing.
Contrast that with “_But I am the greatest motherfucker that you’re ever gonna meet from the top of my head down to the tips of my toes on my feet_” and you get the measure of the man. He’s electrifying.
He’s also humble.
It was a rare treat tonight and I feel honoured to have shared a night with him.
I am a cinephile.
I can easily do difficult movies. Under The Skin. The White Ribbon. Cache. Jeez I can do all the tough stuff.
I am a Mike Leigh-phile too.
Secrets and Lies, Naked, Life is Sweet, Abigail’;s Party, Nuts in May. All brilliant.
I am a Timothy Spall-phile also. (Just too many to mention)
And so I approached Mr Turner with gusto. I like Turner’s seascapes very much. What is there not to like?
It turns out, quite a lot.
To cut to the chase this is one of the dullest 2.5 hours I have spent in a cinema in many a long year. Turgid, plotless, meandering, self-indulgent claptrap of the highest order.
The cinematography has its moments but it takes a lot of moments to make a movie.

There are scenes that are enjoyable, largely in the Royal Academy and one in particular when Constable is ridiculed by Turner but overall it is a study in very dull misogyny that the world is probably no worse without.
Perhaps the most interesting aspect of this movie was the development of his supposed housekeeper Hannah Dandy’s (Dorothy Atkinson) eczema. Was she, or was she not, Turner’s wife/mistress/muse?
Who cares.
Turner-phile ladies sat behind me in the audience and whispered throughout. Damn them.
Utter shite.
Mike Leigh’s worst film by a country mile.
The British Government essentially killed Alan Turing.
The man who invented what we now consider the ‘computer’ and he may have saved 14 million people from death because of his contribution, sorry vast contribution, to the foreshortening of the Second World War through his invention of the Enigma code breaking machine. Churchill thought so.
But, the trouble is, you see, Alan Turing was a homosexual. And the British Government (like many governments today) did not like homosexuals.
Homosexuals in the post war years were lepers of society. So the British Government chemically castrated him. (Better than going to prison for touching a man’s penis? Your call.)
Alan Turing was most likely also a sufferer of Aspergers Syndrome.
He was, in every sense of the word, a genius.
He was not a likeable man because to make real, substantial change sometimes eschews popularity. He was not popular.
It’s a dream role for an actor of substance. That actor is Benedict Cumberbatch.
At the time of writing Cumberbatch has seven movies in production, new episodes of the BBC’s Sherlock and a couple of episodes of The Hollow Crown as Richard III as work in progress. It would seem reasonable to assume from this that he is a man in demand.
Why?
Because he is a brilliant actor. And this is his time. This is most certainly his movie. Yes, he has good support from Keira Knightley, Allen Leech, Matthew Goode and especially Mark Strong, as his ‘boss’. Charles Dance moves on from his movie idol roles into the baddie spotlight and carries it off effortlessly. But make no mistake. This is ALL about Benedict Cumberbatch.
Biopics are often easy meat because they can be imitation games.

# Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes
November 29, 2014 November 29, 2014
Reading _Don Quixote_ has been a year-long project for me in 2014. After reading _Clarissa_ over a twelve month period as part of a readalong in 2012 and then _War and Peace_ in 2013 I decided to tackle another of the very long, intimidating classics on my Classics Club list, this time on my own. Now that I’ve finished I don’t know why I had ever been intimidated by it. Yes, it’s long (over 1,000 pages in most editions) and old (originally published in two parts in 1605 and 1615) and a translation, but I didn’t find it difficult to read at all. It’s fun and imaginative and entertaining – and I loved it.
_Don Quixote_ is the story of a gentleman of La Mancha who has spent so many years reading books of chivalry and romance that he has come to believe the tales they tell are true. Inspired by the heroes of his favourite books, he decides to become a knight errant and go out into the world in search of adventures. Renaming himself Don Quixote and his horse Rocinante, he convinces a neighbouring peasant, Sancho Panza, to join him as his squire. With Sancho at his side, Don Quixote sets out to right wrongs, fight duels and rescue damsels in distress, in the hope that his valiant deeds will win him the love of the beautiful (and largely imaginary) Dulcinea del Toboso.
As Don Quixote and Sancho travel across Spain they have one adventure after another, each one headed with a long and intriguing chapter title such as _“Of the strange adventure which befell the valiant Don Quixote with the bold Knight of the Mirrors”_ or _“Which deals with the adventure of the enchanted head, together with other trivial matters which cannot be left untold”_. As you read on, however, it soon becomes obvious that these ‘adventures’ are not quite as amazing as they sound and usually have a logical explanation.

# Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes
Many people, even without reading the book, will have heard of the famous ‘tilting at windmills’ episode. There are many, many other similar episodes in the novel but this one appears near the beginning which is probably why it’s the best known. If you’re not familiar with it, on approaching some windmills in a field Don Quixote becomes convinced they are giants and attacks them with his sword:
> “What giants?” said Sancho Panza.  
>   
>   
> “Those thou seest there,” answered his master, “with the long arms, and some have them nearly two leagues long.”  
>   
>   
> “Look, your worship,” said Sancho; “what we see there are not giants but windmills, and what seem to be their arms are the sails that, turned by the wind, make the millstone go.”  
>   
>   
> “It is easy to see,” replied Don Quixote, “that thou art not used to this business of adventures; those are giants; and if thou art afraid, away with thee out of this and betake thyself to prayer while I engage them in fierce and unequal combat.”
This is a pattern that is repeated over and over again throughout the novel: Don Quixote mistakes inns for castles and flocks of sheep for armies – and even when Sancho points out the truth he still insists that he is right. The castles and the armies must have been enchanted by great wizards, he says, so that they appear to be inns and sheep. As the story progresses, Don Quixote’s fame spreads and he is thought of as insane and Sancho as an idiot. The response of some of the people they meet can be very cruel and it’s quite sad to see how Don Quixote and Sancho are ridiculed, scorned and made the target of elaborate practical jokes. I wouldn’t describe this as a sad book, though; in fact, it’s a very funny one. The humour doesn’t always work (being four hundred years old and in translation, maybe that’s not surprising) but at times it’s hilarious!

# Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes
As well as the adventures and the humour, there are lots of songs, poems and ballads interspersed with the prose. There are also lots of stories-within-stories – almost everyone they meet on their journey has a long and tragic story of their own to tell – and many of these have no relevance to the rest of the novel. For example, a lot of time is devoted to the tale of a Christian who was held captive by Moors in Algiers and has escaped back to Spain – nothing to do with Don Quixote, but apparently based on Cervantes’ own experiences. This is why the novel is so long and why you need to have some patience with it! Reading this book over a period of several months was the perfect strategy for me as the episodic nature of the story meant that I could leave it for a few weeks and still get straight back into it when I picked it up again. Breaking it up into small sections kept it feeling fresh and interesting so that I never felt bored or overwhelmed.
A quick note on the translation now. There have been many English translations of _Don Quixote_ over the years but not really having any idea which to choose, I started reading the 1885 John Ormsby translation (in the public domain so free to download from Project Gutenberg and other websites) and I found it perfectly readable so decided just to stick with it. I wouldn’t necessarily recommend that translation to everyone as it does use some archaic terms and feels ‘old’ but that’s what I prefer when I’m reading an old book so it wasn’t a problem for me. Whichever may be closest to the literal translation, Ormsby’s description of Don Quixote as “Knight of the Rueful Countenance” just sounds better to me than, for example, Edith Grossman’s “Knight of the Sorrowful Face”. It’s a matter of personal taste, though, so it’s probably a good idea to look at a few different translations and find one that suits you before you embark on such a long novel!
Much as I enjoyed this book it did sometimes feel as if I was never going to finish it, so I was pleased to reach the end. I’m going to miss Don Quixote and Sancho, though, after spending so much time with them this year!

"Scenery" is a novella by contemporary Chinese writer
Fang Fang
, first published in the fifth issue of "Contemporary Writers" in 1987. It is considered by critics to have "lifted the curtain on New Realism".
2
"Scenery" uses Little Eighth Son, who died after only fifteen days of life, as the narrator to describe the emotional desolation and tragic lives of an eleven-member family in a Hankou shantytown. The cruelty of the environment fully unleashes the evil in human nature, with human selfishness and the coldness of interpersonal relationships reaching a shocking level. The novel uses plain and detached language to depict the secular lives of the people living in the Henan Sheds. Their drinking, brawling, scolding, flirting, struggles, and endeavors all reveal folkloric colors through the portrayal of their mundane existence. The father drinking and recounting his war stories, the mother flirting with neighbors, the eldest son wrestling with the father, the second son's heartbreak and suicide, the fifth son's path to wealth, the seventh son being scolded and beaten, scavenging for scraps and picking vegetables, love and marriage—all these episodes showcase the sorrowful struggles of these characters in their fight for survival, demonstrating the author's realist spirit focused on authentic detail.
2
On September 27, 2018, "Scenery" was selected as one of the most influential novels of the 40 years of reform and opening-up.

Seventh Brother said that only when you regard everything in this world, including the world itself, as utterly worthless, do you begin to feel that you have finally tasted the flavor of life; only then can you stride freely and unfettered back and forth along the path of life.

In the past, Father always suspected that Seventh Brother was not his son, because Father was away on a long journey during the period when Mother was pregnant with him. Consequently, Father did not see Seventh Brother for the first time until half a year after his birth. Seventh Brother was skinny and scrawny, bearing no resemblance at all to the tall and robust Father. Father then grabbed Mother by the hair, demanding to know whose son Seventh Brother really was, and Mother responded by quarreling with him at the top of her lungs. Mother was beautiful and flirtatious, but she had indeed never betrayed Father. Only a man like Father could possibly father a son like Seventh Brother. Father only came to understand this truth twenty-five years later, one day after Seventh Brother suddenly announced that he had been transferred to the Provincial Communist Youth League Committee to serve as some sort of official.
Father lived with his wife and their seven sons and two daughters in a thirteen-square-meter wooden-plank house in the Henan Sheds in Hankou. The small room contained one large bed for Father and Mother. The two daughters slept in a tiny attic, while the seven sons slept on makeshift floor beds laid out at night. Over seventeen years in this place, Father and Mother gave birth to their nine children. Their eighth son died half a month after being born. Father was heartbroken and deeply distressed by the premature death of this little life. Father was forty-eight that year. Not only was the newborn the same zodiac sign as him (the Tiger), but he was also born in the same month, on the same day, and at the same hour as Father's birthday. For fifteen days, Father was overjoyed and held his little son every day without fail. He had never bestowed such profound paternal love on any of his other children. However, on the sixteenth day, the infant suddenly suffered convulsions all over his body and then passed away in the evening. Father's expression of grief nearly frightened Mother into fainting. Father bought wood to make a small coffin and buried the infant beneath the window.

That is me. I am profoundly grateful to my father for this flesh and blood he gave me and for allowing me to always stay with my family. I watched my brothers and sisters live and grow up in peace, struggle in hardship, and fight among themselves. Father said Grandfather fled famine from Zhoukou, Henan, to Hankou to work as a dock porter in the twelfth year of the Guangxu era. Grandfather had joined the Red Gang early on and was a skilled fighter for wharf territory. He later died from severe injuries sustained in a fierce battle. From the time he started this line of work, to Fourth Brother, it was already the third generation. Father said he followed Grandfather to fight for the wharf when he was fourteen. Whenever Father recalled those tragic and heroic past events, he would always get very emotional. Every time he drank, he would endlessly recount his war stories. At these moments, all his sons had to sit obediently by his side and listen to his "traditional education." Father now feels somewhat painfully lonely; his children have all flown away one by one, only occasionally returning on Saturday nights. Seventh Brother came home the most often before he got married, yet he loathed and hated this home.
Seventh Brother took over from Fifth Brother and Sixth Brother in collecting scraps when he was five. At seven, Seventh Brother started elementary school. On the very first day, his classmates called him a dirty dog, so his aversion to school and classmates began from that day. Later, Seventh Brother stopped collecting scraps and started skipping school every afternoon to scavenge for vegetables. Seventh Brother met a girl two years older than him named Gougou, so they would always meet by the railway tracks to scavenge for vegetables together. These days became Seventh Brother's most beautiful and kindest days. They flickered with a few faint, brilliant sparks amidst countless thick, pitch-black days. Later, Gougou had an accident while crossing the railway tracks. When Seventh Brother found out, he mustered all his strength and ran frantically towards the railway. His cries of "Gougou" sounded like the wild howl of a starving wolf in the wilderness. But Gougou was gone forever. Seventh Brother fell seriously ill because of this.

When he was little, Seventh Brother thought Eldest Brother was his father because at home, only Eldest Brother didn't treat him like an idiot. Unfortunately, Eldest Brother was rarely at home. As the brothers grew day by day, the floor bed could no longer fit seven men. Father then kicked Seventh Brother under the bed with one foot, while Eldest Brother began working night shifts day after day, month after month, year after year. Eldest Brother was expelled from school in the fourth grade. As soon as he turned fifteen, he entered an ironworks as an apprentice. By twenty, he had become as burly as Father. Later, one day, after Eldest Brother woke up from sleep, he discovered Mother flirting with Bai Liquan next door. Bai Liquan then told Eldest Brother to sleep at his house. As a result, Eldest Brother got Bai's wife, Sister Zhi, pregnant. Bai Liquan came to confront Eldest Brother, and they cursed at each other. Eldest Brother threatened to have Sister Zhi divorce Bai. Bai Liquan sarcastically said that even if Eldest Brother married Sister Zhi, he had nowhere for her to sleep. Eldest Brother suddenly fell silent. Father slapped Eldest Brother and called him useless, so Eldest Brother and Father had a vicious fight. Later, Sister Zhi had an abortion, and from then on, Eldest Brother never paid any attention to Sister Zhi again and looked down on all women, until ten years later when Eldest Brother married his wife.
Seventh Brother hated his elder sisters, Da Xiang and Xiao Xiang, the most. Seventh Brother remembered when he was very, very young and had wet his pants, his elder sister Da Xiang would pinch his buttocks desperately with her fingernails. Xiao Xiang was even more vicious; she forced Seventh Brother to crawl like a dog, and at dinner time, she would tell Father that Seventh Brother was deliberately learning to crawl like a dog instead of walking like a human, so that Father would punish Seventh Brother.
After Eldest Brother fought with Father, the only one in the family who could give Seventh Brother a little warmth was Second Brother. Second Brother always came and went together with Third Brother. One summer, after being beaten by Father, Seventh Brother hid under the bed for a day and a night. Maggots grew in the wound on his thigh, and he fainted, nearly dead.

did not know exactly what intention she harbored. The novella was begun in the summer of 1986. She wrote intermittently, doing other things in between. When she picked up the pen again in early 1987, Fang Fang had already forgotten her initial concept. Fang Fang said that if she had to say something, perhaps she just wanted to tell people: In
Hankou
, there is a place called Henan Sheds; in Henan Sheds, there is "Father's" family. They lived like that in the past, and they still live like this now—not blaming heaven or earth, living roughly and as they please, muddled yet full of flavor. They inherited this way of life from their parents' generation and then passed this legacy on to their children and grandchildren. Of course, there are exceptions, such as Seventh Brother.
Seventh Brother was the traitor among them. Due to the poverty of his family and their low social status, people like Seventh Brother harbored an uncontrollable, even frenzied, impulse to change their own fate, willingly resorting to any means necessary and making sacrifices for it. It was precisely the character of Seventh Brother that became the trigger point for
Fang Fang
writing Scenery.
Thus,
Fang Fang
recalled the poem by
Zuo Si
: "Lush are the pines at the ravine's base, / Sparse are the seedlings on the hill's crest. / With their inch-thick stems, / They shade these hundred-foot boughs. / The high-born tread on lofty positions, / The talented sink to lowly posts. / Their station makes it so, / This has not been for just a day." Despite the passage of fifteen hundred years, reading it today still gave Fang Fang a sense of heaviness. "Station" refers to nothing more than a person's family background and living environment. In contemporary society, the height of one's "station" still holds crucial significance for the rise and fall of their destiny. Individual struggle often appears weak and powerless before "station." Hence, figures like "Seventh Brother" emerge as the times require, swarming forth, becoming people commonly seen in life and attracting a considerable number to draw close to them. With that kind of success, they influence society, forming a cultural phenomenon.
Precisely for this reason,
Fang Fang
wrote the novella "Scenery."
5
Character Introduction

"I" (Little Eighth Son)
"Scenery" employs the voice of "I" (Little Eighth Son), a deceased infant, to narrate the life stories over several decades of a family of eleven living in a thirteen-square-meter shanty by the railway in
Hankou
.
Fang Fang
adopts a unique narrative perspective, that of a departed spirit. "I" died half a month after birth but was particularly favored because "I" shared the same Chinese zodiac sign, the tiger, and the exact same birth date and hour as Father. "I" is a departed spirit who received paternal love, the very paternal love my elder brothers and sisters spent their entire lives longing for. The narrative method of a departed spirit employed by Fang Fang imbues the work with a sense of desolation and vicissitude. Throughout the entire work, there is a tragic force guiding the life trajectories of ordinary characters, which foreshadows the tragic hues in the life paths of the main characters.
7
Eldest Brother
When Seventh Brother was young, he thought Eldest Brother was his father, because at home, only Eldest Brother did not treat him as an idiot. Eldest Brother was rarely at home. As the brothers grew older day by day, the floor bed could no longer accommodate seven grown men, so Eldest Brother began working night shifts all day, all month, all year round. Eldest Brother was expelled from school in the fourth grade, entered an ironworks as an apprentice just after turning fifteen, and by twenty, he was already as burly as Father. Later, one day after waking up, Eldest Brother discovered Mother flirting with the neighbor, Bai Liquan. Bai Liquan then told Eldest Brother to go sleep at his house. As a result, Eldest Brother got Bai's wife, Sister Zhi, pregnant. Bai Liquan came to confront Eldest Brother, and they exchanged insults. Eldest Brother threatened to have Sister Zhi divorce Bai, while Bai Liquan mocked Eldest Brother, saying even if he married Sister Zhi, he had no place for her to sleep. Eldest Brother suddenly fell silent. Father slapped Eldest Brother, calling him useless, so Eldest Brother and Father engaged in a vicious fight. Later, Sister Zhi had an abortion, and from then on, Eldest Brother never paid any attention to Sister Zhi again and scorned all women, until ten years later when he married his wife.
4
Second Brother

Second Brother is a character worth analyzing; his death symbolizes the shattering of beauty and implies the Author's condemnation of the Cultural Revolution era. Second Brother is an anomaly within the family, as the book says, he is "refined and courteous, unlike Father's son," and he is the only family member who brought warmth to Seventh Brother. Second Brother possesses the most intellectual temperament in the entire family, which is primarily reflected in his hope to change his fate through studying, thereby realizing his dream of becoming an architect. However, the outbreak of the Cultural Revolution shattered his dream of attending university, leaving him utterly disheartened. It can be seen that the path of changing one's fate through education was blocked at that time, and anomalous individuals like Second Brother were doomed to be destroyed in that absurd era. Simultaneously, the happy family of Yang Lang, the girl Second Brother loved, was also destroyed during the Cultural Revolution, which similarly reveals the misfortune brought by political movements. Under the successive heavy blows, Second Brother developed a profound sense of desolation and inescapable pain from the depths of his heart; at that time, only love supported his life. Therefore, when he learned that Yang Lang had used her chastity to secure a job placement in the county town and that he had never truly won her love, he chose to commit suicide. However, the book does not solely blame Yang Lang. This prompts readers to understand that, as an educated youth from a well-off family sent to the countryside since childhood, Yang Lang's choice was a matter of necessity at the time. From this, one can perceive the Author's reflection on that era.
6
Third Brother
Third Brother and Second Brother shared the closest bond among the siblings. Second Brother was like a faith to Third Brother—sacred and inviolable. Because Second Brother died over a woman, Third Brother harbored prejudice against women, believing they were unworthy of a man's love, as in his heart, it was a woman who destroyed his faith. During their time in the countryside, Third Brother guarded Second Brother like the most loyal guard, yet he still failed to save Second Brother's life. Deep inside, he was filled with regret and self-reproach. This long-suppressed emotion, having no outlet for release, transformed into hatred towards women. It is precisely this hatred for women that prevented Third Brother from ever finding redemption in his life.
10
Fourth Brother

In the novel, only a small section in Chapter Ten focuses on the life of Fourth Brother, which serves as another critique of the era's absurdity from an opposite perspective. Fourth Brother is both deaf and mute. He married a blind woman, Fourth Sister-in-law, forming a family that appears incomplete but is, in fact, whole. They had children, acquired household goods, and lived a self-sufficient, modest life. Among this family, only the mute Fourth Brother lived a solid and stable life. Specifically, compared to Seventh Brother, who sought power through marriage, Second Brother, who died for love, and the other siblings who were busy with petty schemes, Fourth Brother's life was peaceful and happy. Because Fourth Brother was never beaten by his father and could not hear the filthy language around him, he was better able to preserve the authenticity within his heart. This metaphorically suggests that only those untouched by the harsh realities can live in peace, thereby revealing the filthiness of reality from the opposite angle.
6
Fifth Brother and Sixth Brother
Fifth Brother and Sixth Brother were bad seeds from a young age. They fought, cursed, stole, and even, as children, jointly and brutally gang-raped a girl. These twin brothers grew up tough under their father's whippings and their mother's tyranny. Trains passing every seven minutes, incessant quarrels, and countless punches were the main memories of their childhood. What their childhood left them with most was a character of opportunism and the ability to watch and judge others' moods. As adults, they both became live-in sons-in-law. Since the reform and opening-up, the tide of the commodity economy brought a turning point to their lives, allowing them to successfully transform into members of the self-employed business owners. The joy of overnight wealth went to their heads. The frantic psychology of becoming masters after being oppressed drove them to extremes. Indulging in food, drink, prostitution, and gambling, they began to revel in a life completely different from before, ultimately losing themselves in the playground of desire.
8
Seventh Brother

Seventh Brother is the most extensively depicted character in the novel, embodying multiple layers of metaphorical significance. Seventh Brother's family exhibits a clear power structure, where Father, a dockworker, symbolizes strength, and thus the entire family worships him. Mother needs Father's tenderness after being beaten, and the two elder sisters, to curry favor with Father, engage in gossip and torment the weak Seventh Brother. This bullying behavior reflects the worship of physical force among people at the bottom. Considering such a family environment, it is not difficult to understand the deeply ingrained power consciousness that Seventh Brother carries. The work begins with three consecutive paragraphs initiated by "Seventh Brother said," and at the end, the narrator "I" recalls Seventh Brother's words again, indicating that Seventh Brother now possesses the power of discourse. However, in Seventh Brother's eyes, "the title of professor is utterly worthless." This shows that despite being a university graduate, he lacks identification with the intellectual class. In other words, he has not developed the consciousness of freedom and equality that intellectuals should possess; instead, he clings to the utilitarian philosophy he learned from childhood—"snatching others' nutrients to make oneself lush and green." This implicitly conveys the author's critical stance: when those from the bottom rise to become the powerful, their inherent belief in power is carried into the upper echelons, and the collaboration between the folk and power is not as beautiful as imagined.

In Seventh Brother’s life journey, his university classmate Su Beilao unscrupulously achieved social status, which undoubtedly caused a great impact on his psyche. Recalling his previously tortured life, this naturally intensified his strong desire to change his lowly status. Ultimately, he chose to marry a woman eight years his senior who was unable to bear children, solely because he coveted the high official position of her father. The marriage was merely a transaction, aligning with Seventh Brother’s survival philosophy of changing his fate. Thus, he transformed from the bullied "Little Seventh Son" within his family into a cadre of the provincial Youth League committee, thereby achieving a reversal of his fate. As the work states: "The result of promotion is having social status and power. And the result of having power is a high salary, allocated housing, generous benefits, and respect from all quarters. Only in this way can a person’s fate be most thoroughly changed. Seventh Brother felt that the purpose of his existence was to change his fate." This passage actually implies the author’s writing philosophy: that people from the lower strata, upon gaining power, also acquire money and the capital for ostentation, which runs counter to the purpose of serving the people.
Fang Fang
uses this to sharply critique the bureaucratic system.
6
Impact
After the publication of Scenery in 1987, Fang Fang gained instant fame. The work was considered by literary critics to have heralded the beginning of "New Realism", and Scenery became a representative work of "New Realist Fiction". Fang Fang also became one of the representative writers of the Chinese "New Realism" school.
9
In September 1989, Scenery won the National Outstanding Novella Award for 1987-1988. In the same year, Scenery also received the Jue Shennuxi Cup Award from Selected Novels and the Outstanding Work Award from Selected Novellas.
13
On September 27, 2018, the selection of the most influential novels of the 40 years of China's reform and opening-up, organized by the Selected Novels magazine of the China Writers Association, the Chinese Fiction Society, and the People's Daily Overseas Network, and undertaken by the Qingdao Writers Association, was announced in Qingdao. Scenery was selected as one of the most influential novels of the 40 years of reform and opening-up.
1

Fang Fang at the event for selecting the most influential novels of the 40 years of China's reform and opening-up
Critical Reception
Within its brief length, it portrays the fusion of good and evil in human nature with such profound depth that it can be considered one of the most outstanding works in Chinese contemporary literature of the past thirty years. (Remarks by
Xiuwen Li
, Chairman of the Hubei Provincial Writers Association)
32
Fang Fang's Scenery, as a definitive masterpiece of "New Realism" fiction, fully utilizes the special advantages of the novella form. Through a cross-narration of the death perspective and the omniscient perspective, it presents the chaotic, rough, violent, and hopeless daily life of an underclass family. There, all blood ties and familial affections are trampled by crude human nature, all worldly ethics are stripped away by instinct-driven survival, and the savage growth of life becomes the most helpless scenery of existence. The seeds of a disordered era ultimately grow into weeds in the marginal zones of society; although they cannot find the dignity life should possess, they radiate a tenacious vitality. (Remarks by Hong Zhigang, Professor at the School of Humanities, Hangzhou Normal University)
34
The appearance of Scenery in 1987 is, in retrospect, quite remarkable. For
Fang Fang
herself, it also represents a peak difficult to surpass. The life scenes depicted in Scenery were later termed "underclass narrative," yet Fang Fang's artistic realm far surpasses that of mere "underclass narrative." She observes this world with a compassionate, humanitarian sentiment. Her choice of a deceased infant as the unique narrator seeks a certain possibility of "degree zero." The sense of distance Scenery maintains towards the narrative of suffering is innate, serendipitous, and almost impossible to replicate. In terms of narrative form, Scenery is both modern and realist, thus becoming a landmark work of "New Realism." (Award Citation from the Selection of the Most Influential Novels of China's 40 Years of Reform and Opening-up)
35
Publication Information
"Scenery" was first published in Issue 5, 1987 of Contemporary Writers, and was later included in Fang Fang
's collection of short stories.

"Scenery" is a novella by contemporary Chinese writer
Fang Fang
, first published in the fifth issue of "Contemporary Writers" in 1987. It is considered by critics to have "lifted the curtain on New Realism".
2
"Scenery" uses Little Eighth Son, who died after only fifteen days of life, as the narrator to describe the emotional desolation and tragic lives of an eleven-member family in a Hankou shantytown. The cruelty of the environment fully unleashes the evil in human nature, with human selfishness and the coldness of interpersonal relationships reaching a shocking level. The novel uses plain and detached language to depict the secular lives of the people living in the Henan Sheds. Their drinking, brawling, scolding, flirting, struggles, and endeavors all reveal folkloric colors through the portrayal of their mundane existence. The father drinking and recounting his war stories, the mother flirting with neighbors, the eldest son wrestling with the father, the second son's heartbreak and suicide, the fifth son's path to wealth, the seventh son being scolded and beaten, scavenging for scraps and picking vegetables, love and marriage—all these episodes showcase the sorrowful struggles of these characters in their fight for survival, demonstrating the author's realist spirit focused on authentic detail.
2
On September 27, 2018, "Scenery" was selected as one of the most influential novels of the 40 years of reform and opening-up.

writing Scenery.
Thus,
Fang Fang
recalled the poem by
Zuo Si
: "Lush are the pines at the ravine's base, / Sparse are the seedlings on the hill's crest. / With their inch-thick stems, / They shade these hundred-foot boughs. / The high-born tread on lofty positions, / The talented sink to lowly posts. / Their station makes it so, / This has not been for just a day." Despite the passage of fifteen hundred years, reading it today still gave Fang Fang a sense of heaviness. "Station" refers to nothing more than a person's family background and living environment. In contemporary society, the height of one's "station" still holds crucial significance for the rise and fall of their destiny. Individual struggle often appears weak and powerless before "station." Hence, figures like "Seventh Brother" emerge as the times require, swarming forth, becoming people commonly seen in life and attracting a considerable number to draw close to them. With that kind of success, they influence society, forming a cultural phenomenon.
Precisely for this reason,
Fang Fang
wrote the novella "Scenery."
5
Character Introduction
texts.11:
"I" (Little Eighth Son)
"Scenery" employs the voice of "I" (Little Eighth Son), a deceased infant, to narrate the life stories over several decades of a family of eleven living in a thirteen-square-meter shanty by the railway in
Hankou
.
Fang Fang
adopts a unique narrative perspective, that of a departed spirit. "I" died half a month after birth but was particularly favored because "I" shared the same Chinese zodiac sign, the tiger, and the exact same birth date and hour as Father. "I" is a departed spirit who received paternal love, the very paternal love my elder brothers and sisters spent their entire lives longing for. The narrative method of a departed spirit employed by Fang Fang imbues the work with a sense of desolation and vicissitude. Throughout the entire work, there is a tragic force guiding the life trajectories of ordinary characters, which foreshadows the tragic hues in the life paths of the main characters.
7
Eldest Brother
When Seventh Brother was young, he thought Eldest Brother was his father, because at home, only Eldest Brother did not treat him as an idiot. Eldest Brother was rarely at home. As the brothers grew older day by day, the floor bed could no longer accommodate seven grown men, so Eldest Brother began working night shifts all day, all month, all year round. Eldest Brother was expelled from school in the fourth grade, entered an ironworks as an apprentice just after turning fifteen, and by twenty, he was already as burly as Father. Later, one day after waking up, Eldest Brother discovered Mother flirting with the neighbor, Bai Liquan. Bai Liquan then told Eldest Brother to go sleep at his house. As a result, Eldest Brother got Bai's wife, Sister Zhi, pregnant. Bai Liquan came to confront Eldest Brother, and they exchanged insults. Eldest Brother threatened to have Sister Zhi divorce Bai, while Bai Liquan mocked Eldest Brother, saying even if he married Sister Zhi, he had no place for her to sleep. Eldest Brother suddenly fell silent. Father slapped Eldest Brother, calling him useless, so Eldest Brother and Father engaged in a vicious fight. Later, Sister Zhi had an abortion, and from then on, Eldest Brother never paid any attention to Sister Zhi again and scorned all women, until ten years later when he married his wife.
4
Second Brother
texts.12:
Second Brother is a character worth analyzing; his death symbolizes the shattering of beauty and implies the Author's condemnation of the Cultural Revolution era. Second Brother is an anomaly within the family, as the book says, he is "refined and courteous, unlike Father's son," and he is the only family member who brought warmth to Seventh Brother. Second Brother possesses the most intellectual temperament in the entire family, which is primarily reflected in his hope to change his fate through studying, thereby realizing his dream of becoming an architect. However, the outbreak of the Cultural Revolution shattered his dream of attending university, leaving him utterly disheartened. It can be seen that the path of changing one's fate through education was blocked at that time, and anomalous individuals like Second Brother were doomed to be destroyed in that absurd era. Simultaneously, the happy family of Yang Lang, the girl Second Brother loved, was also destroyed during the Cultural Revolution, which similarly reveals the misfortune brought by political movements. Under the successive heavy blows, Second Brother developed a profound sense of desolation and inescapable pain from the depths of his heart; at that time, only love supported his life. Therefore, when he learned that Yang Lang had used her chastity to secure a job placement in the county town and that he had never truly won her love, he chose to commit suicide. However, the book does not solely blame Yang Lang. This prompts readers to understand that, as an educated youth from a well-off family sent to the countryside since childhood, Yang Lang's choice was a matter of necessity at the time. From this, one can perceive the Author's reflection on that era.
6
Third Brother
Third Brother and Second Brother shared the closest bond among the siblings. Second Brother was like a faith to Third Brother—sacred and inviolable. Because Second Brother died over a woman, Third Brother harbored prejudice against women, believing they were unworthy of a man's love, as in his heart, it was a woman who destroyed his faith. During their time in the countryside, Third Brother guarded Second Brother like the most loyal guard, yet he still failed to save Second Brother's life. Deep inside, he was filled with regret and self-reproach. This long-suppressed emotion, having no outlet for release, transformed into hatred towards women. It is precisely this hatred for women that prevented Third Brother from ever finding redemption in his life.
10
Fourth Brother
texts.13:
In the novel, only a small section in Chapter Ten focuses on the life of Fourth Brother, which serves as another critique of the era's absurdity from an opposite perspective. Fourth Brother is both deaf and mute. He married a blind woman, Fourth Sister-in-law, forming a family that appears incomplete but is, in fact, whole. They had children, acquired household goods, and lived a self-sufficient, modest life. Among this family, only the mute Fourth Brother lived a solid and stable life. Specifically, compared to Seventh Brother, who sought power through marriage, Second Brother, who died for love, and the other siblings who were busy with petty schemes, Fourth Brother's life was peaceful and happy. Because Fourth Brother was never beaten by his father and could not hear the filthy language around him, he was better able to preserve the authenticity within his heart. This metaphorically suggests that only those untouched by the harsh realities can live in peace, thereby revealing the filthiness of reality from the opposite angle.
6
Fifth Brother and Sixth Brother
Fifth Brother and Sixth Brother were bad seeds from a young age. They fought, cursed, stole, and even, as children, jointly and brutally gang-raped a girl. These twin brothers grew up tough under their father's whippings and their mother's tyranny. Trains passing every seven minutes, incessant quarrels, and countless punches were the main memories of their childhood. What their childhood left them with most was a character of opportunism and the ability to watch and judge others' moods. As adults, they both became live-in sons-in-law. Since the reform and opening-up, the tide of the commodity economy brought a turning point to their lives, allowing them to successfully transform into members of the self-employed business owners. The joy of overnight wealth went to their heads. The frantic psychology of becoming masters after being oppressed drove them to extremes. Indulging in food, drink, prostitution, and gambling, they began to revel in a life completely different from before, ultimately losing themselves in the playground of desire.
8
Seventh Brother
texts.21: Seventh Brother is the most extensively depicted character in the novel, embodying multiple layers of metaphorical significance. Seventh Brother's family exhibits a clear power structure, where Father, a dockworker, symbolizes strength, and thus the entire family worships him. Mother needs Father's tenderness after being beaten, and the two elder sisters, to curry favor with Father, engage in gossip and torment the weak Seventh Brother. This bullying behavior reflects the worship of physical force among people at the bottom. Considering such a family environment, it is not difficult to understand the deeply ingrained power consciousness that Seventh Brother carries. The work begins with three consecutive paragraphs initiated by "Seventh Brother said," and at the end, the narrator "I" recalls Seventh Brother's words again, indicating that Seventh Brother now possesses the power of discourse. However, in Seventh Brother's eyes, "the title of professor is utterly worthless." This shows that despite being a university graduate, he lacks identification with the intellectual class. In other words, he has not developed the consciousness of freedom and equality that intellectuals should possess; instead, he clings to the utilitarian philosophy he learned from childhood—"snatching others' nutrients to make oneself lush and green." This implicitly conveys the author's critical stance: when those from the bottom rise to become the powerful, their inherent belief in power is carried into the upper echelons, and the collaboration between the folk and power is not as beautiful as imagined.
texts.22:
In Seventh Brother’s life journey, his university classmate Su Beilao unscrupulously achieved social status, which undoubtedly caused a great impact on his psyche. Recalling his previously tortured life, this naturally intensified his strong desire to change his lowly status. Ultimately, he chose to marry a woman eight years his senior who was unable to bear children, solely because he coveted the high official position of her father. The marriage was merely a transaction, aligning with Seventh Brother’s survival philosophy of changing his fate. Thus, he transformed from the bullied "Little Seventh Son" within his family into a cadre of the provincial Youth League committee, thereby achieving a reversal of his fate. As the work states: "The result of promotion is having social status and power. And the result of having power is a high salary, allocated housing, generous benefits, and respect from all quarters. Only in this way can a person’s fate be most thoroughly changed. Seventh Brother felt that the purpose of his existence was to change his fate." This passage actually implies the author’s writing philosophy: that people from the lower strata, upon gaining power, also acquire money and the capital for ostentation, which runs counter to the purpose of serving the people.
Fang Fang
uses this to sharply critique the bureaucratic system.
6
Impact
After the publication of Scenery in 1987, Fang Fang gained instant fame. The work was considered by literary critics to have heralded the beginning of "New Realism", and Scenery became a representative work of "New Realist Fiction". Fang Fang also became one of the representative writers of the Chinese "New Realism" school.
9
In September 1989, Scenery won the National Outstanding Novella Award for 1987-1988. In the same year, Scenery also received the Jue Shennuxi Cup Award from Selected Novels and the Outstanding Work Award from Selected Novellas.
13
On September 27, 2018, the selection of the most influential novels of the 40 years of China's reform and opening-up, organized by the Selected Novels magazine of the China Writers Association, the Chinese Fiction Society, and the People's Daily Overseas Network, and undertaken by the Qingdao Writers Association, was announced in Qingdao. Scenery was selected as one of the most influential novels of the 40 years of reform and opening-up.
1
texts.23:
Fang Fang at the event for selecting the most influential novels of the 40 years of China's reform and opening-up
Critical Reception
Within its brief length, it portrays the fusion of good and evil in human nature with such profound depth that it can be considered one of the most outstanding works in Chinese contemporary literature of the past thirty years. (Remarks by
Xiuwen Li
, Chairman of the Hubei Provincial Writers Association)
32
Fang Fang's Scenery, as a definitive masterpiece of "New Realism" fiction, fully utilizes the special advantages of the novella form. Through a cross-narration of the death perspective and the omniscient perspective, it presents the chaotic, rough, violent, and hopeless daily life of an underclass family. There, all blood ties and familial affections are trampled by crude human nature, all worldly ethics are stripped away by instinct-driven survival, and the savage growth of life becomes the most helpless scenery of existence. The seeds of a disordered era ultimately grow into weeds in the marginal zones of society; although they cannot find the dignity life should possess, they radiate a tenacious vitality. (Remarks by Hong Zhigang, Professor at the School of Humanities, Hangzhou Normal University)
34
The appearance of Scenery in 1987 is, in retrospect, quite remarkable. For
Fang Fang
herself, it also represents a peak difficult to surpass. The life scenes depicted in Scenery were later termed "underclass narrative," yet Fang Fang's artistic realm far surpasses that of mere "underclass narrative." She observes this world with a compassionate, humanitarian sentiment. Her choice of a deceased infant as the unique narrator seeks a certain possibility of "degree zero." The sense of distance Scenery maintains towards the narrative of suffering is innate, serendipitous, and almost impossible to replicate. In terms of narrative form, Scenery is both modern and realist, thus becoming a landmark work of "New Realism." (Award Citation from the Selection of the Most Influential Novels of China's 40 Years of Reform and Opening-up)
35
Publication Information
"Scenery" was first published in Issue 5, 1987 of Contemporary Writers, and was later included in Fang Fang
's collection of short stories.

"Scenery" uses Little Eighth Son, who died after only fifteen days of life, as the narrator to describe the emotional desolation and tragic lives of an eleven-member family in a Hankou shantytown. The cruelty of the environment fully unleashes the evil in human nature, with human selfishness and the coldness of interpersonal relationships reaching a shocking level. Their drinking, brawling, scolding, flirting, struggles, and endeavors all reveal folkloric colors through the portrayal of their mundane existence. The father drinking and recounting his war stories, the mother flirting with neighbors, the eldest son wrestling with the father, the second son's heartbreak and suicide, the fifth son's path to wealth, the seventh son being scolded and beaten, scavenging for scraps and picking vegetables, love and marriage—all these episodes showcase the sorrowful struggles of these characters in their fight for survival, demonstrating the author's realist spirit focused on authentic detail.

Synopsis
(The following contains plot spoilers; please read with caution.)
Seventh Brother said that only when you regard everything in this world, including the world itself, as utterly worthless, do you begin to feel that you have finally tasted the flavor of life; only then can you stride freely and unfettered back and forth along the path of life.

Seventh Brother is now a somebody. He is very tall and stout, and when dressed in a suit and tie, he cuts an imposing and scholarly figure. Whenever Father meets an acquaintance, he cannot help but mention that his Little Seventh Son once stayed at the Qingchuan Hotel. In the past, Father always suspected that Seventh Brother was not his son, because Father was away on a long journey during the period when Mother was pregnant with him. Consequently, Father did not see Seventh Brother for the first time until half a year after his birth. Seventh Brother was skinny and scrawny, bearing no resemblance at all to the tall and robust Father. Father then grabbed Mother by the hair, demanding to know whose son Seventh Brother really was, and Mother responded by quarreling with him at the top of her lungs. Mother was beautiful and flirtatious, but she had indeed never betrayed Father. Only a man like Father could possibly father a son like Seventh Brother. Father only came to understand this truth twenty-five years later, one day after Seventh Brother suddenly announced that he had been transferred to the Provincial Communist Youth League Committee to serve as some sort of official.
Father lived with his wife and their seven sons and two daughters in a thirteen-square-meter wooden-plank house in the Henan Sheds in Hankou. The small room contained one large bed for Father and Mother. The two daughters slept in a tiny attic, while the seven sons slept on makeshift floor beds laid out at night. Over seventeen years in this place, Father and Mother gave birth to their nine children. Their eighth son died half a month after being born. Father was heartbroken and deeply distressed by the premature death of this little life. Father was forty-eight that year. Not only was the newborn the same zodiac sign as him (the Tiger), but he was also born in the same month, on the same day, and at the same hour as Father's birthday. For fifteen days, Father was overjoyed and held his little son every day without fail. He had never bestowed such profound paternal love on any of his other children. However, on the sixteenth day, the infant suddenly suffered convulsions all over his body and then passed away in the evening. Father's expression of grief nearly frightened Mother into fainting. Father bought wood to make a small coffin and buried the infant beneath the window.

That is me. I am profoundly grateful to my father for this flesh and blood he gave me and for allowing me to always stay with my family. I watched my brothers and sisters live and grow up in peace, struggle in hardship, and fight among themselves. Father said Grandfather fled famine from Zhoukou, Henan, to Hankou to work as a dock porter in the twelfth year of the Guangxu era. Grandfather had joined the Red Gang early on and was a skilled fighter for wharf territory. He later died from severe injuries sustained in a fierce battle. From the time he started this line of work, to Fourth Brother, it was already the third generation. Father said he followed Grandfather to fight for the wharf when he was fourteen. Whenever Father recalled those tragic and heroic past events, he would always get very emotional. Every time he drank, he would endlessly recount his war stories. At these moments, all his sons had to sit obediently by his side and listen to his "traditional education." Father now feels somewhat painfully lonely; his children have all flown away one by one, only occasionally returning on Saturday nights. Seventh Brother came home the most often before he got married, yet he loathed and hated this home.
Seventh Brother took over from Fifth Brother and Sixth Brother in collecting scraps when he was five. At seven, Seventh Brother started elementary school. On the very first day, his classmates called him a dirty dog, so his aversion to school and classmates began from that day. Later, Seventh Brother stopped collecting scraps and started skipping school every afternoon to scavenge for vegetables. Seventh Brother met a girl two years older than him named Gougou, so they would always meet by the railway tracks to scavenge for vegetables together. These days became Seventh Brother's most beautiful and kindest days. They flickered with a few faint, brilliant sparks amidst countless thick, pitch-black days. Later, Gougou had an accident while crossing the railway tracks. When Seventh Brother found out, he mustered all his strength and ran frantically towards the railway. His cries of "Gougou" sounded like the wild howl of a starving wolf in the wilderness. But Gougou was gone forever. Seventh Brother fell seriously ill because of this.

When he was little, Seventh Brother thought Eldest Brother was his father because at home, only Eldest Brother didn't treat him like an idiot. Unfortunately, Eldest Brother was rarely at home. As the brothers grew day by day, the floor bed could no longer fit seven men. Father then kicked Seventh Brother under the bed with one foot, while Eldest Brother began working night shifts day after day, month after month, year after year. Eldest Brother was expelled from school in the fourth grade. As soon as he turned fifteen, he entered an ironworks as an apprentice. By twenty, he had become as burly as Father. Later, one day, after Eldest Brother woke up from sleep, he discovered Mother flirting with Bai Liquan next door. Bai Liquan then told Eldest Brother to sleep at his house. As a result, Eldest Brother got Bai's wife, Sister Zhi, pregnant. Bai Liquan came to confront Eldest Brother, and they cursed at each other. Eldest Brother threatened to have Sister Zhi divorce Bai. Bai Liquan sarcastically said that even if Eldest Brother married Sister Zhi, he had nowhere for her to sleep. Eldest Brother suddenly fell silent. Father slapped Eldest Brother and called him useless, so Eldest Brother and Father had a vicious fight. Later, Sister Zhi had an abortion, and from then on, Eldest Brother never paid any attention to Sister Zhi again and looked down on all women, until ten years later when Eldest Brother married his wife.
Seventh Brother hated his elder sisters, Da Xiang and Xiao Xiang, the most. Seventh Brother remembered when he was very, very young and had wet his pants, his elder sister Da Xiang would pinch his buttocks desperately with her fingernails. Xiao Xiang was even more vicious; she forced Seventh Brother to crawl like a dog, and at dinner time, she would tell Father that Seventh Brother was deliberately learning to crawl like a dog instead of walking like a human, so that Father would punish Seventh Brother.
After Eldest Brother fought with Father, the only one in the family who could give Seventh Brother a little warmth was Second Brother. Second Brother always came and went together with Third Brother. One summer, after being beaten by Father, Seventh Brother hid under the bed for a day and a night. Maggots grew in the wound on his thigh, and he fainted, nearly dead.

When she picked up the pen again in early 1987, Fang Fang had already forgotten her initial concept. Fang Fang said that if she had to say something, perhaps she just wanted to tell people: In
Hankou
, there is a place called Henan Sheds; in Henan Sheds, there is "Father's" family. They lived like that in the past, and they still live like this now—not blaming heaven or earth, living roughly and as they please, muddled yet full of flavor. They inherited this way of life from their parents' generation and then passed this legacy on to their children and grandchildren. Of course, there are exceptions, such as Seventh Brother.
Seventh Brother was the traitor among them. Due to the poverty of his family and their low social status, people like Seventh Brother harbored an uncontrollable, even frenzied, impulse to change their own fate, willingly resorting to any means necessary and making sacrifices for it. recalled the poem by
Zuo Si
: "Lush are the pines at the ravine's base, / Sparse are the seedlings on the hill's crest. / With their inch-thick stems, / They shade these hundred-foot boughs. / The high-born tread on lofty positions, / The talented sink to lowly posts. / Their station makes it so, / This has not been for just a day." Despite the passage of fifteen hundred years, reading it today still gave Fang Fang a sense of heaviness. "Station" refers to nothing more than a person's family background and living environment. In contemporary society, the height of one's "station" still holds crucial significance for the rise and fall of their destiny. Individual struggle often appears weak and powerless before "station." Hence, figures like "Seventh Brother" emerge as the times require, swarming forth, becoming people commonly seen in life and attracting a considerable number to draw close to them. With that kind of success, they influence society, forming a cultural phenomenon.
Precisely for this reason,
Fang Fang
wrote the novella "Scenery."
5
Character Introduction

"I" (Little Eighth Son)
"Scenery" employs the voice of "I" (Little Eighth Son), a deceased infant, to narrate the life stories over several decades of a family of eleven living in a thirteen-square-meter shanty by the railway in
Hankou
.
Fang Fang
adopts a unique narrative perspective, that of a departed spirit. "I" died half a month after birth but was particularly favored because "I" shared the same Chinese zodiac sign, the tiger, and the exact same birth date and hour as Father. "I" is a departed spirit who received paternal love, the very paternal love my elder brothers and sisters spent their entire lives longing for. The narrative method of a departed spirit employed by Fang Fang imbues the work with a sense of desolation and vicissitude. Throughout the entire work, there is a tragic force guiding the life trajectories of ordinary characters, which foreshadows the tragic hues in the life paths of the main characters.
7
Eldest Brother
When Seventh Brother was young, he thought Eldest Brother was his father, because at home, only Eldest Brother did not treat him as an idiot. Eldest Brother was rarely at home. As the brothers grew older day by day, the floor bed could no longer accommodate seven grown men, so Eldest Brother began working night shifts all day, all month, all year round. Eldest Brother was expelled from school in the fourth grade, entered an ironworks as an apprentice just after turning fifteen, and by twenty, he was already as burly as Father. Later, one day after waking up, Eldest Brother discovered Mother flirting with the neighbor, Bai Liquan. Bai Liquan then told Eldest Brother to go sleep at his house. As a result, Eldest Brother got Bai's wife, Sister Zhi, pregnant. Bai Liquan came to confront Eldest Brother, and they exchanged insults. Eldest Brother threatened to have Sister Zhi divorce Bai, while Bai Liquan mocked Eldest Brother, saying even if he married Sister Zhi, he had no place for her to sleep. Eldest Brother suddenly fell silent. Father slapped Eldest Brother, calling him useless, so Eldest Brother and Father engaged in a vicious fight. Later, Sister Zhi had an abortion, and from then on, Eldest Brother never paid any attention to Sister Zhi again and scorned all women, until ten years later when he married his wife.
4
Second Brother

Second Brother is a character worth analyzing; his death symbolizes the shattering of beauty and implies the Author's condemnation of the Cultural Revolution era. Second Brother is an anomaly within the family, as the book says, he is "refined and courteous, unlike Father's son," and he is the only family member who brought warmth to Seventh Brother. Second Brother possesses the most intellectual temperament in the entire family, which is primarily reflected in his hope to change his fate through studying, thereby realizing his dream of becoming an architect. However, the outbreak of the Cultural Revolution shattered his dream of attending university, leaving him utterly disheartened. It can be seen that the path of changing one's fate through education was blocked at that time, and anomalous individuals like Second Brother were doomed to be destroyed in that absurd era. Simultaneously, the happy family of Yang Lang, the girl Second Brother loved, was also destroyed during the Cultural Revolution, which similarly reveals the misfortune brought by political movements. Under the successive heavy blows, Second Brother developed a profound sense of desolation and inescapable pain from the depths of his heart; at that time, only love supported his life. Therefore, when he learned that Yang Lang had used her chastity to secure a job placement in the county town and that he had never truly won her love, he chose to commit suicide. However, the book does not solely blame Yang Lang. This prompts readers to understand that, as an educated youth from a well-off family sent to the countryside since childhood, Yang Lang's choice was a matter of necessity at the time. From this, one can perceive the Author's reflection on that era.
6
Third Brother
Third Brother and Second Brother shared the closest bond among the siblings. Second Brother was like a faith to Third Brother—sacred and inviolable. Because Second Brother died over a woman, Third Brother harbored prejudice against women, believing they were unworthy of a man's love, as in his heart, it was a woman who destroyed his faith. During their time in the countryside, Third Brother guarded Second Brother like the most loyal guard, yet he still failed to save Second Brother's life. Deep inside, he was filled with regret and self-reproach. This long-suppressed emotion, having no outlet for release, transformed into hatred towards women. It is precisely this hatred for women that prevented Third Brother from ever finding redemption in his life.
10
Fourth Brother

In the novel, only a small section in Chapter Ten focuses on the life of Fourth Brother, which serves as another critique of the era's absurdity from an opposite perspective. Fourth Brother is both deaf and mute. He married a blind woman, Fourth Sister-in-law, forming a family that appears incomplete but is, in fact, whole. They had children, acquired household goods, and lived a self-sufficient, modest life. Among this family, only the mute Fourth Brother lived a solid and stable life. Specifically, compared to Seventh Brother, who sought power through marriage, Second Brother, who died for love, and the other siblings who were busy with petty schemes, Fourth Brother's life was peaceful and happy. Because Fourth Brother was never beaten by his father and could not hear the filthy language around him, he was better able to preserve the authenticity within his heart. This metaphorically suggests that only those untouched by the harsh realities can live in peace, thereby revealing the filthiness of reality from the opposite angle.
6
Fifth Brother and Sixth Brother
Fifth Brother and Sixth Brother were bad seeds from a young age. They fought, cursed, stole, and even, as children, jointly and brutally gang-raped a girl. These twin brothers grew up tough under their father's whippings and their mother's tyranny. Trains passing every seven minutes, incessant quarrels, and countless punches were the main memories of their childhood. What their childhood left them with most was a character of opportunism and the ability to watch and judge others' moods. As adults, they both became live-in sons-in-law. Since the reform and opening-up, the tide of the commodity economy brought a turning point to their lives, allowing them to successfully transform into members of the self-employed business owners. The joy of overnight wealth went to their heads. The frantic psychology of becoming masters after being oppressed drove them to extremes. Indulging in food, drink, prostitution, and gambling, they began to revel in a life completely different from before, ultimately losing themselves in the playground of desire.
8
Seventh Brother

Seventh Brother is the most extensively depicted character in the novel, embodying multiple layers of metaphorical significance. Seventh Brother's family exhibits a clear power structure, where Father, a dockworker, symbolizes strength, and thus the entire family worships him. Mother needs Father's tenderness after being beaten, and the two elder sisters, to curry favor with Father, engage in gossip and torment the weak Seventh Brother. This bullying behavior reflects the worship of physical force among people at the bottom. Considering such a family environment, it is not difficult to understand the deeply ingrained power consciousness that Seventh Brother carries. The work begins with three consecutive paragraphs initiated by "Seventh Brother said," and at the end, the narrator "I" recalls Seventh Brother's words again, indicating that Seventh Brother now possesses the power of discourse. However, in Seventh Brother's eyes, "the title of professor is utterly worthless." This shows that despite being a university graduate, he lacks identification with the intellectual class. In other words, he has not developed the consciousness of freedom and equality that intellectuals should possess; instead, he clings to the utilitarian philosophy he learned from childhood—"snatching others' nutrients to make oneself lush and green." This implicitly conveys the author's critical stance: when those from the bottom rise to become the powerful, their inherent belief in power is carried into the upper echelons, and the collaboration between the folk and power is not as beautiful as imagined.

In Seventh Brother’s life journey, his university classmate Su Beilao unscrupulously achieved social status, which undoubtedly caused a great impact on his psyche. Recalling his previously tortured life, this naturally intensified his strong desire to change his lowly status. Ultimately, he chose to marry a woman eight years his senior who was unable to bear children, solely because he coveted the high official position of her father. The marriage was merely a transaction, aligning with Seventh Brother’s survival philosophy of changing his fate. Thus, he transformed from the bullied "Little Seventh Son" within his family into a cadre of the provincial Youth League committee, thereby achieving a reversal of his fate. As the work states: "The result of promotion is having social status and power. And the result of having power is a high salary, allocated housing, generous benefits, and respect from all quarters. Only in this way can a person’s fate be most thoroughly changed. Seventh Brother felt that the purpose of his existence was to change his fate." This passage actually implies the author’s writing philosophy: that people from the lower strata, upon gaining power, also acquire money and the capital for ostentation, which runs counter to the purpose of serving the people.
Fang Fang
uses this to sharply critique the bureaucratic system.
6
Impact
After the publication of Scenery in 1987, Fang Fang gained instant fame. The work was considered by literary critics to have heralded the beginning of "New Realism", and Scenery became a representative work of "New Realist Fiction". Fang Fang also became one of the representative writers of the Chinese "New Realism" school.
9
In September 1989, Scenery won the National Outstanding Novella Award for 1987-1988. In the same year, Scenery also received the Jue Shennuxi Cup Award from Selected Novels and the Outstanding Work Award from Selected Novellas.
13
On September 27, 2018, the selection of the most influential novels of the 40 years of China's reform and opening-up, organized by the Selected Novels magazine of the China Writers Association, the Chinese Fiction Society, and the People's Daily Overseas Network, and undertaken by the Qingdao Writers Association, was announced in Qingdao. Scenery was selected as one of the most influential novels of the 40 years of reform and opening-up.
1

Fang Fang at the event for selecting the most influential novels of the 40 years of China's reform and opening-up
Critical Reception
Within its brief length, it portrays the fusion of good and evil in human nature with such profound depth that it can be considered one of the most outstanding works in Chinese contemporary literature of the past thirty years. (Remarks by
Xiuwen Li
, Chairman of the Hubei Provincial Writers Association)
32
Fang Fang's Scenery, as a definitive masterpiece of "New Realism" fiction, fully utilizes the special advantages of the novella form. Through a cross-narration of the death perspective and the omniscient perspective, it presents the chaotic, rough, violent, and hopeless daily life of an underclass family. There, all blood ties and familial affections are trampled by crude human nature, all worldly ethics are stripped away by instinct-driven survival, and the savage growth of life becomes the most helpless scenery of existence. The seeds of a disordered era ultimately grow into weeds in the marginal zones of society; although they cannot find the dignity life should possess, they radiate a tenacious vitality. (Remarks by Hong Zhigang, Professor at the School of Humanities, Hangzhou Normal University)
34
The appearance of Scenery in 1987 is, in retrospect, quite remarkable. For
Fang Fang
herself, it also represents a peak difficult to surpass. The life scenes depicted in Scenery were later termed "underclass narrative," yet Fang Fang's artistic realm far surpasses that of mere "underclass narrative." She observes this world with a compassionate, humanitarian sentiment. Her choice of a deceased infant as the unique narrator seeks a certain possibility of "degree zero." The sense of distance Scenery maintains towards the narrative of suffering is innate, serendipitous, and almost impossible to replicate. In terms of narrative form, Scenery is both modern and realist, thus becoming a landmark work of "New Realism." (Award Citation from the Selection of the Most Influential Novels of China's 40 Years of Reform and Opening-up)
35
Publication Information
"Scenery" was first published in Issue 5, 1987 of Contemporary Writers, and was later included in Fang Fang
's collection of short stories.

### Awards: DSC for South Asian Literature; Green Carnation
A shortlist has been announced for the $50,000 DSC Prize for South Asian Literature, which was created to "celebrate the rich and varied world of literature in this region and promote the achievements of South Asian writers as well as writers of any ethnicity writing about South Asia and its many diaspora." The winner will be honored January 22 during the ZEE Jaipur Literature Festival. This year's shortlisted titles are:
_The Scatter Here Is Too Great_ by Bilal Tanweer
_The Lowland_ by Jhumpa Lahiri

_The Mirror of Beauty_ by Shamsur Rahman Faruqi
---
Anneliese Mackintosh won the Green Carnation Prize, which is presented "to LGBT writers for any form of the written word, and has a reputation of championing LGBT writers from the U.K.," for _Any Other Mouth_. Chair of the judges Kaite Welsh praised _Any Other Mouth_ as a "a raw, uncompromising debut... that defies categorization. It isn't quite a short story collection or a novel and, as she tells us at the very beginning, it's only almost a memoir. In the end, the only category _Any Other Mouth_ fits neatly into is the one of very, very good books."
